Title: ABC Schedule: ‘High Potential’ Season 3 Sets January Premiere, ‘The Bachelor’ Season 30 Launches in March and More
Main Body Text:
ABC has set premiere dates for its midseason lineup, which notably includes the returns of “ High Potential ,” “ The Bachelor ” and more as well as a new series called “Surviving a Scandal.”

Things kick off on Tuesday Jan. 5, opening with the “Will Trent” Season 5 premiere at 8 p.m. followed by “High Potential” Season 3 at 9 p.m. “High Potential” was the top-rated drama among adults age 18-49 during the 2025-2026 season, meaning it should provide ample lead-in for the program 10 p.m. timeslot: “Surviving a Scandal.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The official description for the newly announced series reads, “From Milli Vanilli to Octomom and Joey Buttafuoco, ‘Surviving a Scandal’ delves into the trials and tribulations of the infamous people whose private lives became tabloid fodder. The series explores the long-term effects of relentless public scrutiny and what happens when your identity becomes synonymous with scandal. Whether thrust into the spotlight for their own scandals, or simply just proximity to foul play, the world watched as one event changed the trajectory of these people’s lives.” Glass Entertainment produces the series for ABC News Studios, with executive producers including Jon Hirsch and Nancy Glass for Glass Entertainment; David Sloan; and Muriel Pearson for ABC News Studios.

Also of note for “High Potential” fans is a special episode airing directly after Super Bowl LXI, which was previously announced to be set on Valentine’s Day.

On Wednesday Jan. 6, “Shifting Gears” has its two-episode Season 3 premiere at 8 p.m. Next is ABC’s longest-running current series, “The Rookie,” with its Season 9 premiere at 9 p.m. followed by the debut of the Jay Ellis-led spinoff “The Rookie: North” at 10 p.m.

On Friday, Jan. 29, “Celebrity Jeopardy” returns for its fifth season at 8 p.m. On Monday, Feb. 1, ABC will air an anniversary special about “American Idol” at 8 p.m. ahead of the Feb. 8 premiere of the singing competition series’ 25th season.

“The Bachelor” will air its Season 30 premiere on March 21 at 8:01 p.m. ABC’s reality dating franchise has been wracked by scandal as of late, with Taylor Frankie Paul’s season of “The Bachelorette” falling apart due to allegations of domestic violence between her and her ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen. Though “Bachelor” series typically run year-round, Season 30 will be the first entry into the franchise since “Bachelor in Paradise” in the summer of 2025. “What Would You Do?” Season 18 will air directly after “The Bachelor.”

ABC also set the midseason returns of series like “9-1-1,” “Grey’s Anatomy” and “Abbott Elementary,” which had their season premieres in the fall. See the full midseason schedule, including previously announced dates for the Grammys and Oscars, below.

Title: Adam Driver Explains Why He’s Starring in Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Reboot After Years of Turning Down MCU Offers: ‘Felt Like the Right Time’
Main Body Text:
Adam Driver opened up about why he said yes to playing Mister Sinister in the “ X-Men ” reboot after turning down many Marvel movies over the years.

“I was a big fan [of ‘X-Men]. I mean, I was a fan of the other things too, but this one felt like the right time,” Driver said during a recent appearance on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” Further reflecting on the reasons he joined the project, Driver added, “It was really ‘X-Men,’ Jake Schreier, who’s the director, his idea for it, and that it’s Kevin Feige . It all kind of came together. The script is really cool.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Driver explained that he was very selective about joining the MCU because “a lot of people are going to watch it, and if it’s bad, you know, a lot of people will see you being bad. Plus, I don’t want to mess it up.”

Marvel head Kevin Feige recently told the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast that he has offered so many Marvel roles to Driver that it has become somewhat of a “tradition” that, when a new project is on the horizon, they meet on Zoom about a part and Driver turns it down.

“It’s no secret we’d like to [work with Adam],” Feige said . “But it’s a tradition to Zoom with him and then he passes. That’s a long-lived tradition. He couldn’t be more cordial. He is usually upfront about how he is feeling.”

In the new “X-Men” film, Driver will play Dr. Nathaniel Essex, aka Mister Sinister, a superintelligent, shape-shifting telepath. As the movie’s main antagonist, he will do battle against Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Inde Navarrette as Rogue, Kit Connor as Cyclops, Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, Maya Boyd as Storm and Asa Germann as Angel.

Title: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’
Main Body Text:
Talk of artificial intelligence tends to float somewhere up in the cloud. “ The Technological Sublime ,” a documentary from director Jannes Callens that heads to the Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ) in Taipei, brings it back down to earth.

The film follows the physical supply chain that keeps AI running, starting at quartz mines in the Appalachians and moving on to Taiwan’s chip plants, Chile’s lithium fields, the cables that run under the sea and the click-workers of Kenya. Along the way, it sets out to show what the technology costs people and the planet. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“I have a fascination with subjects that are hard to visualize,” Callens says. “People tend to talk about AI as if it were something very abstract and invisible, but after doing some research it became clear to me that there is a very tangible ecosystem behind the myth of ‘green’ AI.”

An online image search for AI mostly turns up humanlike robots, he adds, and the absence of pictures of everything underneath pushed him toward the subject.

“This film is first and foremost a work of art that gives me the opportunity to tackle an interesting subject in a truly audiovisual way. I hope to bring some nuance into the AI debate, showing the essence of technological miracles without being blind for the material, ecological and human costs,” Callens says.

Callens’ previous documentary, “Dor (Longing),” about a young man who goes back to Romania to become a shepherd, won the Best Belgian Film award at the Brussels Independent Film Festival and was selected for Visions du Réel. The first scenes of the new film are already shot, and the team is now waiting to lock down the rest of its financing. Callens is meanwhile creating images for a stage play about humanity’s failure to see and face up to the threat of climate change.

Delegate producer Steven Dhoedt has a long-standing interest in new technology. One of his earliest documentaries, “Inside the Metaverse” (2010), looked at the buzz around virtual worlds long before Facebook rebranded as Meta.

“In a similar way, there’s plenty of hype around AI these days, but for a lot of people the technology remains an abstraction,” Dhoedt says. Callens’ take on the subject grabbed him straight away. “Instead of taking the sensational route, the film takes a more timeless, more grounded approach and I strongly believe that this is the type of film about AI we need these days.”

With filming spread across four continents, the producers are still looking for more investors and partners. Belgian broadcaster VRT has boarded the project, and talks are underway with other European broadcasters.

“TCCF gives us a real chance to bring this film to audiences in Asia,” Dhoedt says.

Working with James Chia-Hao Hsu of Reel Asia Pictures, its partner in Taiwan, the team also hopes to start conversations with distributors and sales agents at this stage. The film is a co-production between Brussels-based Visualantics and Cobra Films, Paris-based Tag Film and Taipei-based Reel Asia Pictures.

The Taiwan Creative Content Fest, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), runs Nov. 6–9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.

Title: Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, Unwell Sign With CAA
Main Body Text:
Creative Artists Agency has signed Alex Cooper , Matt Kaplan , and their media and entertainment company Unwell for representation, a move that has been in discussions for weeks.

CAA will work with the duo to expand their business of Unwell, their content company, while supporting  growth and the development of original intellectual property.

Unwell in August announced it had accepted a strategic investment from Patrick Whitesell’s investment firm WTSL, which valued the company at $500 million. Since its founding in 2023, Unwell has expanded into a media and entertainment company focused on Gen Z women. The company, built on the success of Cooper’s “Call Her Daddy” podcast, aims to develop original programming, cultivate emerging talent, and create entertainment and experiences for younger audiences. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Cooper and Kaplan have expanded Unwell’s leadership team over the past year, adding seasoned executives to work alongside Chief Marketing Officer T.J. Marchetti: media and technology veteran Joanne Bradford as President; former NFL and Raine Group executive Samir Sama as Head of Ventures and Corporate Development; previous Meta and Disney executive Mina Lefevre as Chief Content Officer and Head of Television; former Misfits Gaming and Fox Networks Group executive Lagen Nash as Executive Vice President of Revenue; and former CAA agent Olivia Owen as Head of Talent.

Since launching in 2018, Cooper’s podcast has become known for featuring candid conversations with leading figures across entertainment, politics, sports, and culture. The show is distributed through a partnership with SiriusXM, which also powers the Unwell audio channel on SiriusXM’s satellite radio service.

Kaplan is an entrepreneur and film and television producer who has been involved in projects such as “To All The Boys I’ve Loved Before,” “The Perfect Date:” and “Spontaneous.”

Unwell’s slate includes Hulu’s “Call Her Alexc” documentary, a “Hannah Montana” anniversary special for Disney+, and the Netflix property “Let’s Marry Harry.”  Upcoming projects include Netflix’s adaptation of the novel “Icebreaker” and an adaptation of the novel “Deep End.” The Unwell Network has launched seven new programs in 2026  Its YouTube programming includes “Unwell Winter Games” and “Unwell Summer Games,” two reality competition series.

To help steer this growth, Cooper and Kaplan have expanded Unwell’s leadership team over the past year, adding seasoned executives to work alongside Chief Marketing Officer T.J. Marchetti: media and technology veteran Joanne Bradford as President; former NFL and Raine Group executive Samir Sama as Head of Ventures and Corporate Development; previous Meta and Disney executive Mina Lefevre as Chief Content Officer and Head of Television; former Misfits Gaming and Fox Networks Group executive Lagen Nash as Executive Vice President of Revenue; and former CAA agent Olivia Owen as Head of Talent.

Cooper, Kaplan, and Unwell continue to be represented by attorneys Matt Thompson and Emily Zipperstein at Sidley Austin LLP; James Feldman at Lichter Grossman Nichols Feldman Rogal Shikora & Clark; and Shaun Gordon at Weintraub Tobin.

Title: Alex de la Iglesia on His Upcoming Chilean Shoot ‘The Misunderstanding’: ‘Reality Has Become My Parallel World’
Main Body Text:
De la Iglesia presented the film, his first in Chile, at this week's Santiago Film Festival (Sanfic)

At the Santiago Film Festival ( Sanfic ) to talk about his upcoming shoot in Chile, “The Misunderstanding” (“El Malentendido”), Spain’s Alex de la Iglesia (“The Bar,” “30 Coins”) could not have been more effusive. He relates that it was at the festival last year where he met his Chilean producer Pablo Díaz of Rio Estudios (“Hidden Island,” “Berko”) through Sanfic Industria head Gabriela Sandoval. At the same time, he was developing a film in Argentina, where he met his lead, Benjamín Vicuña (“Envious”) who also stars in his upcoming Netflix comedy, “Felicidades.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“In a way, Sanfic set everything in motion and made all of this possible. I also spent time scouting locations back then to get a sense of how the film could be made here. And now, we’re shooting next week,” he told Variety of his first time to film in Chile.

Described as an absurdist comedy combining the Marx Brothers’ farcical humor with the existential anguish of a war film, the titular misunderstanding refers to an incident between two fictitious countries, Lithovenia and Stalovakia, which have been on the brink of war for years. Tensions erupt at the United Nations Assembly when Field Marshal Stroheim storms out after taking offence. Apparently, a perfectly respectful remark — “You look magnificent, strong” — has been misconstrued as “You’re fat.”

“It was a wonderful chain of events, with everything falling into place along the way,” said Díaz who is currently editing his own directorial debut, political thriller “Box 205” (“Habitacíon 205”).

He added: “When I first read Alex’s script, my immediate thought was that we could recreate all the battle scenes here in Chile. We have the right landscapes to offer excellent locations for the trenches, barracks and everything involved in the battle sequences. But when Alex came for a location scout in June or July, he also fell in love with downtown Santiago.”

Plans for the next four weeks is to shoot at some mansions in Santiago, including the former U.S. embassy, and outside the city to the create the battlefield with trenches.

Vicuña, who plays a hapless Minister of Foreign Affairs, agreed: “It’s lovely to look at it that way: as a series of fortunate events, one leading to another. Because, ultimately, getting a film made is a small but extraordinary miracle, isn’t it? Bringing together the right people, securing the resources—all the pieces have to fall into place.”

“Perhaps this project was simply meant to happen, and perhaps there is a real need to talk about war today. It’s a film that will resonate with audiences and challenge them to reflect. In that sense, I’m just one more link in this chain of fortunate events and good news that made the film possible.”

Holding forth at the press conference, de la Iglesia, whose Pokeepsie Films produces alongside Rio Estudios, noted: “The story reflects something we are all experiencing today: a sense of chaos, bewilderment and absurdity in the world around us. It feels as though the world is being run by madmen, terrible people—or perhaps they’re simply incompetent. Or are they monsters? Who are these people?”

“I’ve chosen to portray them, in part, as deeply stupid. I think there is an enormous amount of incompetence, as there is in every aspect of life, but here its consequences are magnified because the stakes are so enormous.”

“As you grow older, reality seems to increasingly resemble what goes on inside your head. You begin to question whether the world has changed or simply whether you’re seeing it through a distorted lens. Perhaps we don’t just observe reality; we reshape it through our own perceptions.”

He added: “I’ve always used my work as a way of protecting myself from life’s hardships – from pain, anxiety, and boredom. My profession allows me to build a parallel world through which I can make sense of reality. But now, with the world in its current state, that has become increasingly difficult, because reality itself has turned into my parallel world.”

The rest of the cast includes Maria Barranco (“Harikiri, I Miss You”), Mona Martínez (“Terminator: Dark Fate”), Hugo Silva (“The Body”), Fernando Tejero (“The Captive”), Oscar Casas (“Idols”) and Miguel Rellán (“Spanish Shame”).

“The Misunderstanding” is backed by Spanish broadcaster RTVE, streamer Movistar+ and Beta Entertainment.

Title: Bear Grylls Speaks Out on Russell Brand Verdict After Helping Baptize Him: ‘Justice Has Now Been Served’ and the Victims Are ‘Heroes’
Main Body Text:
Bear Grylls , the adventurer and TV host known for “Man vs. Wild,” has spoken out about Russell Brand ‘s rape and sexual assault conviction after he helped to baptize him in 2024.

Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in his highly publicized London criminal trial. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. Brand pleaded not guilty and has denied all allegations. After the ruling, Brand was taken into police custody to await his sentencing on Monday. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Grylls made headlines back in 2024 when he was present for Brand’s baptism in the River Thames, less than a year after the initial allegations against Brand were exposed in the Sunday Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches” docuseries. Brand was previously a guest on Grylls’ show “Running Wild” in 2023, before the docuseries was released. After the allegations came out, Brand converted to Christianity and spoke about his religion extensively on his social media channels.

In a post on X Friday reacting to the verdict, Grylls said: “Brand’s faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism. I have attended a few now. Even visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes. It’s part of our calling as men and women of faith, to love and serve anyone. It is the sick that need healing. Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn’t want to ever discourage someone’s coming to faith.”

However, he added, “It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”

Six women testified against Brand in the trial about alleged incidents that occurred between 1999 and 2009. After the verdict was read, the Metropolitan Police announced that they are currently investigating further rape allegations against Brand from two women.

Title: Blackpink’s Jisoo Signs With WME for Worldwide Representation
Main Body Text:
Jisoo , the singer and actor best known as a member of K-pop group Blackpink , has signed with talent agency WME , which will represent her worldwide.

The deal comes as Jisoo builds out her solo music career. Last week she released “Addicted,” a moody dance-pop number about being powerless against attraction. The track has hit the top of iTunes Top Songs charts across 28 regions and also led the iTunes Worldwide Songs chart. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“Addicted” is the follow-up to “Click,” which was billed as her first pre-album single. That song, a pop track, centers on two people from very different backgrounds who find their way to each other.

Jisoo has also kept busy outside the recording studio in 2026. Earlier this year she completed Blackpink’s Deadline World Tour, a sold-out run that played stadiums across North America, Europe and Asia. She headlined “Boyfriend on Demand,” a Netflix rom-com series that debuted in March, and made her first Met Gala appearance in May. She also teamed with Off-White and Pokémon on brand collaborations.

Jisoo first went solo in 2023 with her debut EP “Me,” which set a South Korean benchmark as the first record by a female soloist there to top 1 million in sales. Its breakout single “Flower” climbed to No. 2 on the Billboard Global 200 and went one better on the Global Excl. U.S. chart, where it hit No. 1. The music video drew the biggest 24-hour audience of any K-pop video released that year.

She followed with the 2025 mini album “Amortage,” featuring the tracks “Earthquake” and “Your Love.” Last year she also released “Eyes Closed,” a collaboration with Zayn that became her second solo release to crack the Top 10 of Billboard’s Global Excl. U.S. chart. The song also charted at No. 20 on the Global 200, while on the Hot 100 it peaked at No. 72.

WME’s music division counts Adele, Billie Eilish, Bruno Mars, Coldplay, Olivia Rodrigo, Rihanna, Shakira and The Weeknd among its clients.

Title: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stomps to $6.7 Million in Previews
Main Body Text:
Everyone’s favorite kaiju is stomping its way back to the box office.

“ Godzilla Minus Zero ,” the sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” has made $6.7 million in previews. The Japanese movie is expected to beat fellow newcomers at the box office this weekend with a $30 million opening. That’s more than double the $11.4 million opening that “Godzilla Minus One” had three years ago. The first movie, also written and directed by Takashi Yamazaki, charged its way to $57 domestically, becoming the biggest live-action Japanese movie in North America, and $113 million globally. It also was the surprise winner of the visual effects Oscar, beating out big-budget, CGI spectacles like “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,” “Mission Impossible: Dead Reckoning,” “Napoleon” and “The Creator.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Yamazaki’s sequel keeps setting records for the monster series. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is also the first Japanese movie ever filmed for Imax, where it should over-perform as premium large formats have exploded this year thanks to “The Odyssey.” The sequel, produced by Japan’s Toho and distributed in the U.S. by GKids, takes place two years after “Minus One” as Godzilla returns and a new monster arrives.

This weekend’s other new movies will be no match for Godzilla. Warner Bros. Animation’s new take on “The Cat in the Hat,” starring Bill Hader, made $1 million in previews and is expected to come in second place with $20 million. Searchlight and director Martin McDonagh’s dark buddy comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, made $900,000 in previews and is on track to make $4 million to $7 million in limited release. Finally, the Indian epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” released by Sony in North America, made $3.5 million from its Thursday opening and Wednesday previews and is  projected to open with $6 million.

Title: Bradley Cooper and Danny McBride’s ‘G.I. Joe’ Movie Set for 2028; Paramount Shifts New ‘Paranormal Activity’ to Halloween 2027
Main Body Text:
Danny McBride ‘s “G.I. Joe” movie, starring Bradley Cooper , will march into movie theaters in 2028.

Paramount announced on Friday that the film will get a wide theatrical release on Oct. 20, 2028. McBride will direct the reimagining of the “G.I. Joe” franchise — which kicked off with the Hasbro toy line and spawned comic book series, animated series and a trio of live-action films — from a screenplay he wrote with Jeff Fradley and John Carcieri. Cooper is set to star as Duke , one of the franchise’s most iconic characters, but the studio is keeping further plot details under wraps. The film is produced by Lorenzo di Bonaventura, Mark Vahradian, and Zev Foreman for Hasbro Entertainment. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Paramount and (the newly-renamed ) Blumhouse Atomic also revealed that the next “ Paranormal Activity ” movie will debut in the Halloween corridor (on Oct. 22, 2027), instead of launching in the summer. The film, directed by Ian Tuason, was previously dated for May 21.

Created by Oren Peli, the original “Paranormal Activity” grossed nearly $194 million worldwide and became one of the most profitable films in cinema history. The found-footage franchise has since grown to seven installments and grossed more than $900 million globally.

The new movie stars Chase Yi, Sonia Mena and Maya Da Costa. Peli returns to produce for Solana Films, with James Wan and Jason Blum producing for Blumhouse Atomic. Michael Clear and Judson Scott will executive produce for Blumhouse Atomic, with Alayna Glasthal overseeing the project for the company. Executive producers are Steven Schneider (for Room 101, Inc.), Dan Slater and Cody Calahan.

The dating announcements come as Skydance, led by David Ellison, focuses on maximizing its massive IP library after the major consolidation united Paramount and Warner Bros. One example: the mega-studio recently announced there’s a new “Transformers” project in the works, with Steven Spielberg attached to steer the franchise as a producer. Paramount was already developing “Top Gun,” “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles,” “Sonic the Hedgehog” and “Star Trek” sequels, while Warner Bros. is set to deliver an “Ocean’s 11″ prequel (directed by Cooper who co-stars with producer Margot Robbie), more “Lord of the Rings” movies and the “Weapons” sequel “Gladys,” as the combined studio commits to release 30 movies a year.

Title: Cannes, Annecy-Winning ‘Iron Boy’ Producer Eddy Cinema Backs Memory-Erasure Animation ‘Wilderness of the Greenriver’ at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
Main Body Text:
A man who has no memory of his past finds out that a patient is the sister he lost in “ Wilderness of the Greenriver ,” an animated feature from Barcelona-based Hong Kong director Ellis Kayin Chan that is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ) in Taipei.

The film is set in a world where technology lets people wipe out painful memories. When Arin learns that a patient named Zia is his sister, the discovery shakes what he believes and unlocks memories of a childhood he had forgotten. He has to decide whether to uphold the system or embrace his own humanity. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The story is rooted in Chan’s own loss. He says the film grew from a simple conviction: “Pain is not the enemy of being human – forgetting is.”

“I grew up believing that if I stayed calm, if I didn’t feel too much, I could stay safe. When my sister and I grew apart, I tried to erase the pain connected to her. What I didn’t realize was that I was also erasing the tenderness, the care, the love that had shaped who I was,” Chan says. “When I received the news that she had taken her own life, everything I had buried came back at once. I cried like a child. My heart hurt in a way I couldn’t control. And in that moment, I understood something very clearly: pain was not what destroyed me. Pain was what proved that love had existed.”

He adds that the film does not romanticize suffering. “It asks a quieter, more uncomfortable question: if we remove pain to survive, what parts of ourselves do we also erase?”

A Gobelins graduate, Chan recently worked as animation supervisor on “Lost in Starlight,” Netflix’s first Korean animated feature, and has done work for Burberry and Balenciaga. His short films include “Monsoon Blue” and “Bluebird in the Wind.”

The project has already picked up honors. A three-minute proof of concept was made with support from the Hong Kong Arts Development Council. In 2025, it took home the top award at Taipei’s Golden Horse Film Project Promotion (FPP), with the prize money going toward writing and development, and at Annecy this year it picked up awards from Ciclic, SACD and Titra in the feature pitches.

Chan is now turning the treatment into a screenplay with writer Clément Roussier, aiming to finish the script in early 2027. Storyboard, casting and editing are slated to wrap by early 2028, animation will run from 2028 into 2029 and a theatrical release is planned for 2030.

The film is produced by Paris-based Eddy Cinéma, one of whose founding members, Nicolas de Rosanbo, serves as executive producer. The company co-produced Louis Clichy’s “ Iron Boy ,” which won a Special Jury Prize in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section and the jury and audience awards at Annecy this year, and has worked with Chan since he left Gobelins.

“We have long admired the strong direction, delicate artwork and poetic writing which characterize Ellis’s work, and are delighted to collaborate with him on his first feature,” the producers say.

They see the film as a hopeful story about family and the ethics of technology, with appeal for both family audiences and arthouse viewers. “We believe the film will have a strong market potential in Europe and Asia,” they say.

In Taipei, the team is looking for co-production partners in Asia, animation studios, and distributors and sales companies.

The Taiwan Creative Content Fest, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), runs Nov. 6–9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.

Title: Comcast Co-Founder Julian Brodsky Dies at 93
Main Body Text:
Julian Brodsky , a cable TV pioneer and financial guru who was a co-founding partner of Comcast more than 60 years ago, has died. He was 93.

Comcast announced his death Friday. According to the cable and media company, Brodsky died peacefully surrounded by his family while in hospice care on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.

Brodsky teamed with Comcast founder Ralph J. Roberts and co-founding partner Daniel Aaron to build the company from its earliest days, beginning with the acquisition of a small cable television system in Tupelo, Mississippi, in 1963. Working from a “modest office” near Philadelphia, the three laid the foundation for what would grow into one of the world’s leading media and technology companies, according to Comcast. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“Julian was an extraordinary leader, a brilliant financial mind and one of the architects of cable television,” Brian L. Roberts, chairman of Comcast, said in a statement. “He was a trusted partner and close friend to my father, Ralph, and someone I was fortunate to learn from and work alongside for so many years. He was one of the most creative financiers of his generation, but just as important, he established a culture of financial integrity, uncompromising standards, and respect for colleagues that remains at the heart of our company today.”

Roberts added, “Julian was a mentor and a friend, and his contributions to our company and our community cannot be overstated. We will miss him deeply, and our thoughts are with his family and everyone who knew and loved him.”

Brodsky was born in Philadelphia on July 16, 1933. He attended Overbrook High School and graduated from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. He served two years in the U.S. Army before beginning his career as a certified public accountant. While working as an auditor, he developed an early fascination with the emerging cable television industry, an interest that would shape the course of his career and help define his legacy.

As Comcast’s longtime CFO, Brodsky was instrumental in financing the company’s expansion and efforts to raise capital. The company credits him with helping guide major acquisitions that transformed Comcast from a small regional cable operator into an industry leader. Brodsky was among the industry’s “earliest financial innovators,” according to Comcast, helping establish cable television’s credibility as an investment and demonstrating its long-term potential to banks, institutional investors and Wall Street at a time when the business was still in its infancy.

Brodsky played a central role in Comcast’s initial public offering in 1972 and helped establish the company’s reputation for financial integrity and disciplined management, the company said. Along with Ralph Roberts, he formed Comcast Interactive Capital in 1999, now called Comcast Ventures, to invest in early-stage technology companies and obtain a window into opportunities that could potentially benefit Comcast’s business. In 2004, Brodsky became Comcast’s non-executive vice chairman and retired from the company and its board of directors in 2011.

Brodksy’s contributions to the cable television industry were recognized with numerous honors, including his induction into the Cable Television Hall of Fame in 2003 and the National Cable & Telecommunications Association’s Distinguished Vanguard Award.

Beyond Comcast, Brodsky was a dedicated philanthropist and a champion of the Philadelphia community. Together with his beloved wife of 70 years, Lois, he supported numerous cultural and educational institutions, including the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where he served for nearly three decades as a trustee. In October 2026, the couple announced a $20 million gift to establish the Lois G. and Julian A. Brodsky Learning and Engagement Center, reflecting their longstanding commitment to making art and education accessible to future generations.

In addition to Lois, Brodsky is survived by their three daughters, Debra Brodsky, Ellen Brodsky (married to Ted Rybeck) and Laura Brodsky (Michael Beard), and his brother, Marc Brodsky (Vivian Brodsky). He was predeceased by his parents, David and Esther Brodsky. He is also survived by four grandchildren.

A private memorial service will be held, and a celebration of Brodsky’s life will be announced at a later date.

Title: Fox Commits to Carrying Non-Fox Content on Roku for at Least 3 Years as DOJ Closes Antitrust Investigation
Main Body Text:
The Department of Justice’s Antitrust Division Friday announced that it closed its investigation into Fox Corp.’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku after finding the deal “is not likely to result in harm to competition.”

However, Fox — which announced the completion of the Roku deal Friday — made several commitments to the DOJ in connection with the deal.

According to the DOJ, “Consistent with the Division’s finding that the transaction is unlikely to result in harm to competition, Fox has committed that Roku will remain an open and neutral content partner post-merger.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Specifically, Fox has committed to abide by the following four conditions:

The DOJ’s Antitrust Division opened an investigation into Fox’s proposed Roku acquisition, as is customary, and in September issued second requests for documentation to Fox and Roku. According to the agency, the division “analyzed whether the proposed merger may harm competition among free, ad-supported streaming providers” and “considered whether Fox might use its control of the Roku platform to disadvantage its content rivals post-merger.”

The Justice Department concluded that Fox’s Roku takeover would be “unlikely” to introduce “substantial risk of harm.”

“The Division concluded that the entry of free, ad-supported streaming providers would be timely, likely, and sufficient to make a substantial risk of harm to competition unlikely,” it said in its statement. “Additionally, the investigation found that, because Roku relies on a broad offering of content from many providers to attract consumers, the merged firm would suffer monetary and reputational harm if it attempted to use the Roku platform to harm Fox’s content rivals. If the merged firm were to degrade the Roku platform, consumers could switch to other connected TV platforms.”

The DOJ said the Antitrust Division will “continue to evaluate competition in the industry and may take appropriate action in light of changing facts or circumstances.”

It’s true that if Fox were to discriminate against TV and streaming rivals in deals for the Roku platform, that would hurt Roku’s existing business. In the first nine months of 2026, Roku has topped financial forecasts , delivering 23% revenue growth for the period to hit $4.1 billion in sales. About 49% of that came from advertising and 40% is from subscriptions.

Fox Corp. has consistently promised to continue to run Roku as an “open ecosystem” following the merger since it announced the agreement in June 2026.

“Beginning today, our top priority for the combined company is to continue to relentlessly serve audiences and partners, while reinforcing the openness and choice that is the essence of the Roku platform,” Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch said in a statement Friday.

Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood is joining Fox Corp. as co-chair alongside Paul Cheesbrough of Fox Digital Platforms, a newly formed division housing Roku, Tubi, Fox One, Red Seat Ventures and other digital businesses. With the completion of Fox’s Roku acquisition, several execs are departing , including Roku Media president Charlie Collier and Tubi CEO Anjali Sud.

Title: Fox’s Paul Cheesbrough Will Expand Duties After Roku Deal; Anjali Sud, Charlie Collier to Exit
Main Body Text:
Paul Cheesbrough , a one-time software engineer who has worked to transform upstart digital ventures at Fox Corp. into mainstream operations, is taking on an important new role at the company following its $22 billion purchase of Roku .

Cheesbrough was named co-chair and CEO of Fox Digital Platforms on Friday, a division that will house Roku operations, Tubi and Red Seat Ventures, among other operations and turbocharge the company’s new-media ambitions. Roku operates one of the primary portals consumers use to access their favorite programming via streaming and broadband. Anthony Wood, the founder of Roku and previously its chairman and CEO, will become a member of the Fox board and serve as co-chair alongside Cheesbrough. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“Together we have premium live sports and news, a growing streaming portfolio, and a leading connected TV platform,” Cheesbrough and Wood said in a memo Friday. “More importantly, we have talented teams who know how to build, innovate, and deliver for viewers, partners, and advertisers. We have a lot to celebrate — and a lot to build.”

Under a new structure outlined Friday, the new unit of Fox Corp. will be built around Roku, to be led by CEO Mustafa Ozgen; direct-to-consumer properties like Tubi, Fox One and Frndly TV, led by CEO Pete Distad; and Red Seat Ventures and financial-technology company Credible, which will be led respectively by CEO Chris Balfe and CEO Robert Humann.

Several senior executives are leaving the combined company. Charlie Collier, the president of Roku Media, who worked to develop the company’s original content and advertising operations, will exit, as will Chris Handman, Roku’s general counsel, and Robyn Peterson, executive vice president at AdRise, a connected TV ad-tech platform owned by Fox Corp.

Others are taking on new roles. Mike Bidgoli is being promoted to president of Tubi, reporting to Distad, following a decision by Anjali Sud, CEO of Tubi, to take “a new role outside the company,” according to the memo. She will assist through a transition period. Andy Karofsky, co-founder and CEO of Frndly TV, a live streaming service, will also report to Distad. Lisa Holme, head of content for the Roku Channel, will report to Distad as well.

Melody Hildebrandt will continue as chief technology officer of Fox Corp. Jeff Dow, Fox’s executive vice president of platform and media technology, will retire at the end of the fiscal year. Ad sales will report to Jeff Collins, president of ad sales for Fox.

Cheesbrough, who got his start as a software engineer working for IBM, has shown a proclivity for digital media, having developed digital products for the BBC and Telegraph Media Group before joining News Corp, a sibling of Fox that is also run by its controlling shareholders, the Murdoch family. He previously served as Fox Corp.’s chief technology officer and president of digital, and has presided over a methodical turn by the company, perhaps best known for Fox News Channel and the Fox broadcast network, into direct-to-consumer operations and content pacts with independent hosts.

“We won’t have every answer on Day 1,” the executive said in the staff memo. “We’ll share decisions as they’re made, be clear about what’s still open, and keep moving. Our priorities remain the same: build great products, serve our viewers and partners, and support each other.”

Title: Gay Influencer Famed for Dancing in High Heels Faces Middle Age in Nine-Year Taiwan Creative Content Fest Documentary ‘My Silly Flirty Boys’
Main Body Text:
A gay influencer in Taiwan who became famous dancing in high heels, and the filmmaker who trained his camera on him for nine years, both stare down middle age in “ My Silly Flirty Boys .”

The documentary from Taiwan-based Hong Kong filmmaker Frankie Sin is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

Sin followed Fufu from 2017 to 2026. Over that stretch, Fufu built a following with racy dance routines, performances in high heels and his online channel “FJ234,” where he talked openly about desire and helped bring drag queens and other LGBTQ+ performers to mainstream audiences. Not everyone approved. Critics who wanted gay men presented in a more respectable light branded him a “cancer of the gay community.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Away from the spotlight, Fufu talks frankly about what fame has cost him and about the loneliness that sets in once the persona comes off. Now nearing 40, he is coming to terms with a face and body that are getting older.

“It began with my own anxiety over my queer identity and feeling out of place within the community’s mainstream standards, which led me to point my camera at a maverick who dared to challenge sexual taboos,” Sin says.

More than 10 years ago, Sin swapped one of Hong Kong’s conservative outlying islands for Taiwan, hoping its reputation for openness would give him a place to belong. What he found instead was a local gay scene that prized hyper-masculinity and a “model gay” image.

“This triggered a second wave of anxiety about my body and identity,” Sin says. “In 2016, I met Fufu, an influencer famous for dancing in high heels. His bold, confident display of desire stood in sharp contrast to my own insecurities and repression. He became a mirror for me.”

The shoot spans the years around Taiwan’s legalization of same-sex marriage and charts how queer entertainment grew and was then swallowed up by the mainstream market.

“As two gay men approaching 40 – one losing his spotlight, the other confronting his deepest insecurities – we both face a midlife crisis, learning how to make peace with aging, loneliness, and ourselves,” Sin says.

Fufu’s channel is shutting down this year, and with nearly all the key footage shot, the team is logging nine years of material ahead of a rough cut. Color grading, the sound mix, an original score and music clearances will follow, with picture lock targeted for the third quarter of 2027.

Stefano Centini and Chuti Chang serve as executive producers, with Henry Leong and Peter Yam producing. The producers say the film takes an honest look at the pecking order and shared anxiety inside Taiwan’s gay male community.

“By placing the personal changes of both men alongside the rise and fall of Taiwan’s queer entertainment industry, the film offers a rare, honest perspective with strong potential for cross-cultural resonance,” they say.

In Taipei, the team is looking for gap financing to finish post. It also wants to meet co-producers and sales agents from abroad, plus festival programmers, to help plan a worldwide release.

Sin is also developing two more feature documentaries about belonging and family. “An Island Boy” follows a young Hong Kong fisherman, while “Nomads of the Island” explores Sin’s own family history.

The Taiwan Creative Content Fest, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), runs Nov. 6–9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.

Title: Golshifteh Farahani, Renate Reinsve and Alicia Vikander Lead Torino’s Female Talent Charge
Main Body Text:
For the second year running, 10 of the 16 films in Torino’s feature competition are directed by women

Known for championing first and second features, the Torino Film Festival has increasingly become a showcase for rising female talent.

For the second year running, 10 of the 16 films in Torino’s feature competition are directed by women, a proportion now matched by this year’s short-film selection. While few festivals, in Italy or elsewhere, can match Torino’s level of inclusion, artistic director Giulio Base is adamant that such results “have nothing to do with quotas.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“This is part of a worldwide trend in the film industry,” says Base. “Women are already doing great work, so it’s not about percentages. I only care about good films, and there are plenty of them.”

Of course, a familiar face never hurts, and Torino’s competition boasts more star power than most. Itonje Søimer Guttormsen’s “Butterfly,” starring Renate Reinsve , Chabname Zariab’s “When She Hears the Bells,” starring Golshifteh Farahani , and Rachel Rose’s “The Last Day,” led by Alicia Vikander and Wagner Moura, all see established arthouse names lending their profiles to emerging female filmmakers.

Meanwhile, recent festival breakouts like Muriel D’Ansembourg’s “Truly Naked,” Sarah Arnold’s “Too Many Beasts” and Amira Duynhouwer’s “Sugar” reflect the curatorial freedom of a festival less preoccupied with bragging rights.

“I’m not obsessed with securing world premieres,” Base explains. “I don’t think the Turin public goes around the world’s festivals saying, ‘I’ve already seen it.’ I’d rather choose the strongest films out there.”

To sift through more than 5,000 submissions, Base assembled a gender-balanced selection committee, recruiting every member before they turned 30. He sees that generational mix as essential.

“Ultimately, the question of women comes down to who’s watching the films,” Base explains. “I’m the old guy, so I want fresh eyes on work coming in from all over the world. When the six young men and women and I sit down to discuss the selections, I realize we all watch differently, and I always benefit from the exchange.”

All the same, Torino has decisively leaned in, marking its 44th edition with three women-led juries. Director Francesca Archibugi (“Vivere”) will chair the feature competition, while film legend Stefania Casini (“1900,” “Suspiria”) oversees the documentary competition and pop culture icon Chiara Francini (“Miracle at St. Anna,” “Drag Race Italia”) handles shorts. The festival will also enlist an all-female roster of journalists and academics to introduce films in this year’s Marilyn Monroe retrospective.

“Marilyn was so often seen as a sensual object,” Base says. “For me, it’s important that 24 women share their perspectives to show that she was so much more than that.”

This year’s selection spans 120 titles across six sections. True to its mission as a showcase for emerging talent, and its origins as the Festival Internazionale Cinema Giovani (literally, the Festival of Young Cinema), stories of youth abound. Asked which films resonate with him personally (“It’s not good for a director to pick favorites, but I’m human and I have my preferences”), Base singles out recent TIFF winner “Thirteen in Gaza,” by Palestinian filmmaker Hosam Abu Da, and “Good People,” a documentary by Venice Golden Lion winner Milcho Manchevski.

“The title already says a lot,” Base says of “Thirteen in Gaza.”

“[‘Thirteen in Gaza’] was the first film shot and completed in Gaza in 12 years. I think it’s important to hear voices like this, even if the director can’t attend for the reasons we all know. People shouldn’t miss this one.”

Base is even more emphatic about Manchevski’s documentary, calling it “probably the film that affected me most during this selection process.”

“It’s about a disco in Macedonia that caught fire about 20 months ago, much like the one in Crans-Montana on New Year’s Eve,” says Base. “I don’t know how many young people perished in that fire, but the people he interviewed gave such touching, unsensationalized testimony about what it was like to be there. It’s a great documentary, and enormously moving.”

Looking ahead, Base, who holds a doctorate in theology, stays true to himself when asked about his goals.

“I’m a dreamer,” he says. “I’d like to take the festival to the top of the charts. That’s what we’re trying to build and that’s our ambition. It’s not easy, because we have maybe a tenth of what the big festivals have, but sometimes David beats Goliath.”

Title: Helene Hahn Loyd, Executive With Disney and DreamWorks, Dies at 78
Main Body Text:
Helene Hahn Loyd, the executive who was part of the executive team that built DreamWorks SKG and was instrumental in Disney’s renaissance of the 1980s and ’90s, died Oct. 24 in Park City,  Utah. She was 78.

Born Helene Bulakoff in Westbury, New York, she graduated from Hofstra University and moved to Los Angeles. She started her career with a temp job at Paramount Pictures while she was attending law school, and earned her degree from Loyola Law School in 1975. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Returning to Paramount, she rose to senior vice president and earned a reputation as a formidable dealmaker. At Walt Disney Studios, she was named executive vice president in 1981, becoming one of the most high-ranking women in the film business at the time.

Working with Jeffrey Katzenberg, she helped engineer the studio’s comeback, including its partnership with Pixar. In 1994, she was recruited to help build DreamWorks SKG, and served as its chief operating officer.

She was a passionate mentor to upcoming female executives.

After moving to Park City, she “approached skiing with the same ferocity she applied to dealmaking,” her official obit stated.

Her husband of over two decades, Charles “Chuck” Loyd Jr., died in July.

Title: Hollywood Has Flipped on GenAI, Says ‘Avatar’ VFX House Weta FX Chief: ‘If You Don’t Have an AI Strategy, Don’t Bother’
Main Body Text:
Major Hollywood studios have gone from banning generative AI outright to shunning visual effects vendors that lack an AI plan, according to Daniel Seah , CEO of “The Lord of the Rings” and “ Avatar ” VFX house Weta FX .

Seah spoke to press in Taipei on Friday, after Weta FX signed a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF). Weta’s clients, he said, are mainly the Big Four studios and the streaming platforms. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“We also got the memo from each of the studios, especially from their legal departments, saying that there is no such scenario that you can use any of GenAI for any of our work,” Seah said of early last year. By the middle of the year, several clients were allowing it, provided Weta got pre-approval and worked with only a small number of companies. Around the turn of the year, clients began asking about Weta’s AI strategy, mostly to find out how much money the technology could save.

“It’s, ‘If you don’t have an AI strategy, don’t bother to work with us,’” Seah said of the period since the third quarter of this year.

That shift drove Weta to look for a partner that could help it move faster on GenAI. It found one in Taiwanese animation and VFX outfit Moonshine Studio, which it has worked with for around six months. Seah said AI had become a national strategy in Taiwan on the back of the island’s semiconductor industry. Moonshine, without the client restrictions Weta faced, had been moving quickly as a result, he said.

Seah said Weta has no intention of using AI to replace any of its artists or employees. “It’s more like to enhance and increase more workflow for us,” he said.

Weta chief technology officer Kimball Thurston said the company has been building its own AI models for modifying and recreating the world, “not necessarily the like ChatGPT-type of model.” Work with Moonshine is likely to focus on the artist layer – what the AI world calls the harness, “which I think is the worst name they could have chosen,” Thurston said. The goal is a tool that lets people refine their stories across “whole timelines of long-form content rather than just 20-second TikTok videos.”

Thurston also said Weta uses outside video models such as Kling AI and ByteDance’s Seedance where clients permit it. “You kind of have to,” he said. “It’s not every studio allows us to, but they also came onto the scene and killed a bunch of competition, fundamentally.” Security rules mean such models must be hosted outside China, he added. That is achievable, he said, because ByteDance now operates globally.

Under the partnership, TAICCA and Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture will identify young talent and introduce them to Weta FX. Weta may offer them internships at its offices in Wellington, Melbourne and Vancouver. Seah said Weta recently announced it is likely to open a representative office in London too.

“There’s a Taiwan contingent at Weta in Wellington already,” Thurston said. He added that those artists were there before the new deal and are “integral members of the crews.”

Weta has no footprint in Taiwan. Seah called the island the ideal base for exploring Asia. He pointed to flight times of three to four hours to Southeast Asia, Japan and Korea, government backing and a pool of engineers and storytellers. Thurston said Weta has also spoken to people in Thailand and Korea. He also pointed to a build-out of immersive experiences across Asia, possibly via Singapore.

“It’s more, to me, about market enablement than it is about any particular location,” Thurston said.

“I think this is a key opportunity to move from technology hardware to technology applications – that is, software,” TAICCA chair Sue Wang added. She called the deal the biggest Taiwan has struck in the content industry so far.

Thurston said Weta started an open-source project around 18 months ago called the Rongotai Model Train Club, named after an area of Wellington. The project tracks refinement and LoRA training and writes that usage into image metadata. Anyone defining a model has to state which datasets were used. Thurston said the effort dovetails with work at the Visual Effects Society’s Technology Committee and at MovieLabs.

In the past year, Thurston said, Weta won a data center design award for the Southern Hemisphere. The award was for a cooling system that uses no water and is more power-efficient.

“I hate that a lot of companies are building up gas, basically gas turbines to power data centers,” Thurston said. “I think it represents bad engineering, speaking as a computer scientist.”

Weta VFX supervisor Sheldon Stopsack said the new tools have to fit into the studio’s existing pipeline, including its motion-capture work. “We want to be able to kind of shape the world the way the filmmaker envisioned it, we envisioned it, and, you know, have this creative control ultimately at the end of the day with any of these technologies,” Stopsack said.

“People still want to see the big star performing,” Thurston added. “They may be performing as an ape, or they may be performing as a Na’vi, or some other crazy creature that gets created, and that creature may be created using some technique, but people want to go see the actor perform.”

Title: Jane Fonda ‘Didn’t Dare Imagine’ Democrats’ Blue Tsunami: ‘We Have to Block What’s Bad and Fight For What’s Good’
Main Body Text:
Senior Editor, Culture and Events

Jane Fonda was giddy Thursday night at the Women in Film Honors gala in Beverly Hills.

“I’m so excited,” she told me while practically skipping down the red carpet.

The longtime political activist is riding the Election Day blue wave that helped the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“I felt pretty optimistic, but I didn’t dare imagine that it would be this broad,” Fonda said. “I’m just so proud of American people, that they were paying attention and it wasn’t just about affordability. [James] Talarico’s acceptance speech was a masterpiece and in it he said, ‘We voted to love our neighbor.’”

She added, “I’m so excited with how many incredible women have been elected to high important offices.”

As for the Democrats’ next move, Fonda said, “We have to be very smart. We can’t return to the old neoliberalism. We have to take off our corporate hat, take off our donor hat, and start doing things that are going to help working people in this country, and we have to rule with love. We don’t rule yet, but we have to block what’s bad and fight for what’s good.”

She continued, “It’s not just about accountability and investigations because there’s so much corruption and criminality, but it also has to be about really putting power in the hands of working people and making life better for them.”

Talking to Jane Fonda just two days after Election Day. Jane Fonda ‘Didn’t Dare Imagine’ Democrats’ Blue Tsunami: ‘We Have to Block What’s Bad and Fight For What’s Good’ MORE: https://t.co/Kyvp5XG966 via @variety #justforvariety pic.twitter.com/NlYOWaZT2y

Fonda said she knows a lot of the candidates who won their elections. “I have a PAC and I’ve been traveling the country meeting them. These are different kinds of people,” she said. “People are just pissed. They don’t want crime. They don’t want chaos. They don’t want corruption.”

Fonda was on hand at the gala to help honor Salma Hayek, who received the Jane Fonda Humanitarian Award.

Kerry Washington told me that she watched the election results on the news with her family. “I didn’t cry on Tuesday night, but on Wednesday when I woke up, it kind of hit me,” she said. “I think the reason I cried on Wednesday was because I realized how many people voted who had never voted before. It felt to me the big wave that matters is that more people than ever before are understanding that their vote matters. Look at what’s happening in Mississippi right now, and there’s no way to look at that race and not understand that every single vote counts.”

As of Thursday afternoon, Democrat Scott Colom held a lead of 1,813 votes over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican serving her first term, according to the New York Times.

Title: Jesse Eisenberg and Julianne Moore on ‘The Debut,’ Testing AI to ‘Make Sure It’s Bad’ and Hoping ‘Now You See Me 4’ Gets Made
Main Body Text:
Awards Circuit Podcast: The roundtable discusses the “Blue Tsunami” on Election Day, and the movies still to come.

Jesse Eisenberg has a confession about the biggest moment in “The Debut.”

When the crowd at the Telluride world premiere broke into mid-film applause after a showdown between Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, also known as “the rent is due” scene, his first thought wasn’t relief.

“Oh no! Can they go on the ride?” he recalls to Variety . That’s because the next scene is dramatic. “If you’re a paranoid and worried person, all signs lead to panic.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

That’s the man who wrote, directed, produced, scored and stars in the A24 musical comedy, which has taken awards season by storm. He also built the entire film around his muse, Oscar winner Julianne Moore, who plays Mona Friedman, a shy housewife who picks up a flyer and auditions for a community theater musical for the first time in her life. Eisenberg wrote the role for her.

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit podcast , we sit down with the two collaborators to discuss their latest film, their anxieties about the future of the industry and Eisenberg’s hopes for another “Now You See Me” sequel. Listen below!

Moore has been nominated for five Academy Awards — supporting actress for “Boogie Nights” (1997) and “The Hours” (2002) and lead actress for “The End of the Affair” (1999), “Far From Heaven” (2002) and “Still Alice” (2014), winning for the latter. Eisenberg was nominated for best actor for his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in David Fincher’s “The Social Network” (2010) and for best original screenplay for “A Real Pain” (2024), which won supporting actor for Kieran Culkin.

A24’s “The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival to rave reviews. It has since played the Toronto, New York and Middleburg Film Festivals, the latter of which is where this podcast episode was recorded.

Moore has spent decades as Todd Haynes’ muse. Now she belongs to Eisenberg, too. When I ask whether he’s warned Haynes off, he says jokingly, “He gets it.” Eisenberg’s explanation for why directors keep coming back to her is one of the best cases for her career I’ve heard in a while. He gets “pissed off” reading reviews of “May December” that praise its depth and darkness without recognizing what he sees: “an unbelievably brilliant comic creation.” She has, he says, “a funny bone within drama that is so unusual,” the kind drama school trains out of you.

A24 opens “The Debut” in theaters on Dec. 11

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Eisenberg : Oh my God, of course. You hope there’s some sentient reaction from the audience. But there’s another weird thing that’s less expected. When you’re working on a movie, you’re working on it for two or three years and everybody you’re working with is an ally. No one’s criticizing it or poking holes in it, except in good-natured ways. It’s, “Can we try this? Can we try that?” So you forget that it’s going to be critiqued, and you forget that it could be a disaster because you’ve spent three years with people who all love it. At that point, this little moment of panic creeps in because you realize this whole thing could have been for naught. So the fact that there was a great reaction to it, an audible reaction, is a kind of relief.

Eisenberg : I have such paranoia that my first thought after it gets huge applause and laughter is, “Oh no! Can they go on the ride?” Because the next scene is dramatic. If you’re a paranoid and worried person, all signs lead to panic.

Moore : She was completely original, and so original on the page. It’s an extraordinary feat of writing and character development that Jesse just handed me. I’m so lucky to embody someone right on the brink of change. She’s relatable because she’s all of us who’ve been in a place where we know we want something different, but we don’t know what it is and we’re willing to take a chance. What leads her to that place? Why does she pick up that flyer and audition for the first time in her life? She’s following a desire without knowing where it will lead her. She doesn’t know anything. She’s so literal in her understanding, and she goes on a complete voyage of character development, finding community, meaning and purpose. Mona, in a sense, is any of us who’ve tried something new.

Eisenberg : That’s such a nice and perceptive question. I didn’t think I wanted the audience to be off balance. All I wanted to do was create a subjective story. Because the movie is about the world of musical theater, it gave me permission to make a heightened movie, because we’re living in that theme and tone. So whatever Julianne is feeling in a particular scene is heightened 20% in that direction. If she’s feeling scared, she’s walking past people warming their hands over a garbage can fire in this fantastical-looking, terrifying 1920s version of a city. If she’s feeling welcomed, then it’s Halle Bailey, the world’s sweetest person and loveliest actress, coming to tell her, “I know we’ve just met, but I can tell we’re going to be sisters.” I wanted everything to be filtered through this woman, who’s a baby and has experienced such invisibility. That’s why it sometimes feels fantastical in a positive way, with Halle, who’s wonderful in the movie and sometimes overly terrifying, like the scenes with Paul Giamatti, who’s a genius. It’s all about what she’s feeling, not objective reality.

Eisenberg : When we were looking for titles for this movie, my friend suggested “Rent” because it’s a musical and it’s all about her getting the rent.

Eisenberg : I think we looked into it. No, it would be too comic.

Eisenberg : I will say … he gets it.

Moore : First of all, oh my God, thank you. It’s unbelievably flattering to be called someone’s muse. It’s unbelievably rewarding to spark someone’s imagination and to think you’ve been part of their creative process in any way. That’s the most magnificent thing as an actor: having a real collaboration. That’s what we’re all about. Jesse wrote a movie about a creative journey and where it happens, and it happens in community. It happens with another person. We don’t do what we do alone. We can’t. It’s even reflected in the relationship with Paul’s character. People talk about him being an antagonist, an adversary. He’s not at all. He’s her creative partner. He grows with her, and at a certain point, he has to say, “Now you’re on your own. Now you perform. I’ve taught you as much as I can teach you, and now you go.” It’s everything I’ve ever wanted in my career: to have people who want to work with me and to somehow add to their work as well.

I’m always saying I got one shot at this, and if we do it again, then OK, now I know I can do it.

Moore : I was jealous, though, because he said, “I’m doing this movie.” He had already written “A Real Pain” and was on his way to make it when we finished “When You Finish Saving the World.” I’m like, “There’s not a part for me in it?”

Eisenberg : It’s funny that you brought up her being a muse for people because, while you were asking, I was trying to think about what that means. It’s something quite specific. It’s not just that this person is phenomenal and famous, and it certainly has nothing to do with “Oh, she can help me get my movie financed.”

Moore : And I don’t know that I can.

Eisenberg : It’s purely creative. There’s something so unbelievably funny about her that I find gets overlooked when I read notices about her movies, because she’s also this glamorous, phenomenal dramatic actress. I always get pissed off when I read responses to “May December.” Everybody’s like, “This wonderful performance, so rich in depth and darkness.” It is all those things. But I watch it as an unbelievably brilliant comic creation. “Far From Heaven,” again, another dramatic thing, but there’s such humor in the repression she’s experiencing. Maybe that’s why people love her so much. She has a funny bone within drama that’s so unusual, because you go to drama school and they don’t encourage you to be funny.

Eisenberg : Exactly, and don’t you dare compromise the stakes by having a funny bone. She’s so naturally funny without ever being a comic, and it’s so rare. I think for people like Todd Haynes, who I don’t know that well but know is funny, that’s a real joy.

Moore : Jesse’s wonderful about putting stakes in real life. So often, I read screenplays and the only way they’re able to create stakes is through a murder, a missing child or an asteroid that’s going to hit the Earth. Yes, obviously there are stakes involved in that, but there are stakes in everyday life. Is somebody going to call you? Is the meeting going to go well? Are you going to burn dinner? There are stakes, and they matter to us. The fact that Jesse can invest his films with those kinds of emotional stakes is really interesting to me, because I think that’s how we live. That’s who we are.

Eisenberg : Also, with the asteroid stuff, anybody would react the same way, which is panic. Whereas, if you have a real character, they’re putting life-and-death stakes on something the rest of us might not agree with. She wants to be in this play. I think 90% of people, if Paul Giamatti yelled at you on the first day of rehearsal, would just quit the show. But because this person is coming into this world with so little, she ends up imbuing this silly thing with life-and-death stakes and then we can relate.

Moore : I loved it. I thought it was so funny as written, and I was also worried it would be distracting. So how do you imbue this action with enough meaning that it’s equally funny but not distracting when you’re trying to do something emotional? Oddly, it’s her first engagement in an imaginary circumstance, which is what they teach you in acting. How do you make something real when it’s not real? How do you make an audience believe it’s really happening? If you make the audience believe it, they won’t laugh. You can laugh at it from out there, but when you see her doing it and making it real, it won’t distract from the emotional content. It’s something you do when you’re first starting out: stir a pot, open a door, button a shirt. You’re pretending, but it has to be exact and you have to believe it, too. I did say to Jesse when he was putting it together, “Is it distracting? Is the smoking weird?” He was like, “Nope. It’s perfect.”

Eisenberg : It’s also a woman discovering her sensuality — not sexuality, but sensuality — where she’s starting to feel things in her body. She’s drinking. It’s what happens to an actor. You try to open yourself up to sensuality.

Moore : I think we all tend to look forward, not back. When you’re living your life, you’re just like, “What’s next? What’s in front of me? What am I working on? What am I eating next? When’s breakfast?” You don’t reflect on what you’ve done, and sometimes, as people mention it, you’re like, “Oh, yeah, that movie.” Something odd happens. You construct something, and then you forget it in performance as well, because there’s an unconscious aspect to performing. You want to be prepared enough that when you’re actually doing it, you lose consciousness of your actions and that in itself leads to forgetting. Sometimes, if I see things I’ve done, I’m like, “I don’t remember doing that with my head or walking that way or making that vocal choice.” You do it, and then it’s behind you. I never think about it. I’m just grateful that I have something to do, because that’s what propels me. What am I doing? What am I engaged in?

Eisenberg : It’s funny to hear Julianne Moore, and I’m using your full name on purpose, talk about just looking forward, because her career has touched so many people and contributed so much to culture. I feel the same way, and I see it as fear. What will I be doing next? What will I work on? Part of the reason I’m doing so many different things isn’t just because I have this amazing, creative, expansive mind. It’s because I’m kind of terrified that none of them will work out. Doing five jobs on this movie is how I protect myself for the future. I can be a writer if you want that, or I can go direct a deodorant ad or something and, worst case, I can promise you I can do it because I did “The Debut.” I have that feeling about everything. We’re in an unstable industry, and I don’t do well with instability in general.

I’ve been thrust into this job, which I’m very lucky to have, but it’s not a good job for my personality and wiring. My counter to that is to try to do as many things as possible. And I am unpretentious. The next movie I want to do more than anything is “Now You See Me 4,” and I’m praying that they write it, because I love that more than anything. I don’t have this feeling that, now that I’m directing these more independent, serious movies, I don’t want to be in something a little more Hollywood-ish. I like working. I feel so lucky to have done what I do, and I feel so hopeful that I get to do it more.

Moore : I was thinking about this just this morning. Creatives keep appearing. I was thinking about talking to young people because I’m going to do a master class at SCAD when I’m down there. A friend I worked with a long time ago runs the department. What do you say to students? What I always say is, “These are your peers. Look around. You’re going to be working with these people. Your creative life starts now.” People keep emerging, and we always act surprised. “Oh my God, look at this filmmaker.” But they were there. Here they come. You don’t know that the 22-year-old you spoke to at SCAD will be the next big filmmaker in 10 years. People talk about the business, but it’s really about the stories people are telling. What are they writing? What are they directing? Where are these actors coming from? They keep being born.

Moore : Absolutely not. This charming, wonderful young actor emerged in “Roger Dodger” and people were like, “Look at this kid.” You were what, 17?

Moore : So his acting career started then, but no one would have said, “Oh, he’s going to be a really important filmmaker.” And yet, there he was.

Eisenberg : I have a paranoid answer for this. I’m totally paranoid. I sometimes experiment with AI to see whether it’s good at writing. And it’s still not. I’m paranoid, so I check and it still isn’t. Thank God. I say, “Write a scene like this.” I’m just testing it to make sure it’s bad, and it’s still bad. So I’m relieved, but, like, how far away is it from being good? How far are we from a kid putting on a pair of goggles and saying, “I want to watch a movie about me where I rob a bank and then kiss the girl I’m in love with at school. Here are pictures of her, here are pictures of me” and then they press play? I’m paranoid about that.

The saving grace is two things. One is what Julianne said: Creative spirit will find ways to entertain and delight us and speak about things in a way that maybe computers won’t. The other thing I think about all the time, and she’s about to go to a play in New York, is that I do these Greek plays, which were written 2,500 years ago and we perform them the same way they were performed 2,500 years ago. If they’ve lasted that long, they’ll still be there. People want to be in the same room as other people, watching and listening to stories. It’s as old as cave people sitting by the campfire telling stories, and there will always be room for that. What I do worry about is whether we’ll still be able to make a living from it. I’m not 100% sure about that.

10 QUESTIONS WITH JULIANNE MOORE & JESSE EISENBERG

Eisenberg : This is not ironic: “Wild Thing,” because I was a really rambunctious basketball player. I’m not joking. If you meet somebody who knows me, they’ll know.

Moore : Witchcraft. I just loved witchcraft. I used to buy books on the occult and cast spells and stuff.

Eisenberg : Wrestling. Loved wrestling.

Moore : I’ve never done karaoke in my life. In the shower, stuff from “Dear Evan Hansen.”

Eisenberg : My karaoke song was “Hold On Loosely” by .38 Special, and in the shower, it would be “Rose’s Turn” from “Gypsy.” Somewhere in the middle is where I live.

Eisenberg : We just talked about that. “Rent.”

Moore : Or “No One Cares.” That was the original title. That’s what we filmed it under.

Eisenberg : I do more voice work than people expect. My kid and I do really great impressions. I don’t think those will make it into a multiplex, but I do some pretty funny voice work.

Moore : Vanilla. Soft-serve vanilla. It’s not a brand. But now it gives me a stomachache, so I’ve really got to watch it as we get older. Can I also say that this is my second favorite, and everyone thinks it’s disgusting? Rum raisin.

Eisenberg : For me, it’s pistachio, only because I am a paranoid person and eating ice cream makes me feel like I’m doing something bad for my body. If I have the illusion that it’s derived from nuts, it makes me feel calm. I’ve had rum raisin once, and it’s delicious.

Eisenberg : Maybe “Seinfeld.” But who would I be? I’d be the boy.

Moore : You can be an extra. You don’t have to be one of the main ones.

Eisenberg : Could I start with a cop-out? Mona Friedman. I watch that, and I’m like, “That’s me.” Everything is me in her.

Moore : Countess Olenska, because she’s so self-sacrificing. I admire her, but I don’t know that I could do it.

Eisenberg : Bob Odenkirk screamed at me for writing commercial romantic comedies when I was 21 and said, “You’re a thoughtful young person. Be an artist. Write something personal.” It changed my whole life.
