Title: Joaquin Phoenix Stars in AI Eyewear Campaign Directed by Jonathan Glazer
Main Body Text:
Gentle Monster's intelligent eyewear collection will be available for pre-order Nov. 12.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Joaquin Phoenix is entering the world of wearable AI.

The Oscar-winning actor stars in a new campaign film for Gentle Monster’s upcoming intelligent eyewear collection , directed by “The Zone of Interest” filmmaker Jonathan Glazer . The South Korean eyewear brand unveiled a first-look teaser Friday, ahead of the collection’s Nov. 12 pre-order launch.

The surreal short film follows a salesman, played by Phoenix, who encounters a series of bizarre occurrences inside an unfamiliar hotel. He then comes face-to-face with mysterious figures at the end of a red-lit corridor, eventually discovering that his intelligent eyewear allows him to understand and communicate with them. The full film is scheduled to debut later this month. Related Stories CMAs Photo Gallery: See Taylor Swift, Ella Langley, Kacey Musgraves, Lainey Wilson, Stella Lefty and Other Stars on the Carpet and On-Stage Taylor Swift to Perform at CMAs for the First Time in 13 Years

The collection is part of a larger partnership between Gentle Monster, Google and Samsung, first unveiled at Google I/O in May. Built on Google’s Android XR platform and powered by its Gemini AI assistant, the smart glasses promise to offer hands-free assistance, allowing users to take photos, make calls and translate conversations.

Fashion and technology companies have been trying to make AI-powered wearables the next “big thing” for a while. The wave continued with Meta and Ray-Ban’s second generation of AI glasses endorsed by Kylie Jenner earlier this year. Meanwhile, luxury conglomerate Kering, whose portfolio includes Gucci and Saint Laurent, has partnered with Google to develop its own AI-powered eyewear. In April, Kering CEO Luca de Meo said the company was targeting a 2027 debut for Gucci-branded smart glasses.

Pre-orders for the Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear Collection begin Nov. 12, followed by a public preview in New York from Nov. 13 to 23. Registration for the preview will be available through the brand’s website.

Title: Katherine Ryan Feeling ‘Grief and Relief’ Over Russell Brand Conviction After Reportedly Calling Out His Behavior on Comedy Central
Main Body Text:
Years after Katherine Ryan reportedly confronted Russell Brand about alleged predatory behavior while working alongside him on Comedy Central’s “Roast Battle” in 2018, the comedian has spoken out following his conviction on rape and sexual assault charges.

“It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain,” Ryan said on the latest episode of her podcast “Telling Everybody Everything.” “They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The Canadian comedian said she and other women had been privately processing the verdict, which she described as bringing both a sense of justice and renewed grief for those affected.

“I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today,” she said. “There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”

She continued: “Everything’s nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened.”

Ryan previously made headlines in 2022 when she told Louis Theroux in his BBC documentary series that she had confronted an unnamed male comedian about his alleged predatory behavior. During the interview, Ryan said she had worked alongside a man on a television program and called him a “predator,” describing the potential legal repercussions as a “litigious minefield.”

Her comments fueled speculation that she was referring to Brand. Ryan has never publicly confirmed the identity of the comedian she was discussing.

Brand, 51, was found guilty Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial at London’s Southwark Crown Court. He was acquitted of two additional rape charges and one count of indecent assault. The comedian, who denied all allegations of non-consensual sexual activity, is scheduled to be sentenced on Monday.

Title: Leo Reich on Capturing Gen Z Angst in ‘It Gets Worse,’ Scoring a Lena Dunham Cameo and Having ‘Loads of Ideas’ for a Potential Season 2
Main Body Text:
Leo Reich can’t seem to shake London.

Born and raised north of the river, the 28-year-old comedian, actor and writer moved east a few years ago — and it’s probably the furthest he’ll venture from home.

“I wish I could be one of these people who’s like, ‘I’m going to go live in Spain for a year.’ I’m not,” Reich admits at a hip coffee shop around the corner from his flat, sipping on an iced latte despite the dropping temperature. To cope, he’s sporting a red Vivienne Westwood scarf over a simple black jean jacket and white T-shirt. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

To his credit, Reich did once try out New York City for a month and a half in the early days of his stand-up career. He’d grown up a fan of movies and shows set in the Big Apple — “Frances Ha,” “Girls,” “30 Rock” — but it didn’t live up to his expectations. “Because I was kind of this pretentious teenager, I was like, ‘I gotta move to New York in my 20s, it’s going to be fucking incredible.’ And then I eventually went and I was like, ‘This sucks.’ They didn’t get me!”

Luckily, Reich’s hometown has provided the perfect backdrop for “ It Gets Worse ,” the comedy series he wrote and stars in that also marks A24 ‘s debut U.K.-made show. “Everyone I’ve ever met is here,” he says of London. “It’s perfect.”

Judging from our one hour at the coffee shop, this isn’t that much of an exaggeration. Reich is approached twice, once by a friend and once by a stranger, both gushing with praise about “It Gets Worse.” “I haven’t laughed out loud like that in ages!” a 20-something girl excitedly tells Reich. “Amazing work.”

When we meet, the show has been out in the U.K (via Channel 4) for just six days, but Reich has already been surprised by the enthusiastic reception and rave reviews from The Guardian, The Times and more. And on Friday, it will premiere across the pond on Paramount+. “So far it’s been such a nice, warm reaction for a show that is, I would say, at points really unbearable to watch,” Reich says with a laugh.

Inspired by his favorite American shows, including “Girls,” the comedy follows three best friends and roommates — Ethan (Reich), Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray) — as they navigate their 20s in London after moving out of their shared flat. It possesses that dry, awkward, self-deprecating British humor that is clearly shared by its author, along with a healthy dose of pessimism (as is implied by its title). The result is a hilarious, all-too-real depiction of the existential angst that has come to plague Gen Z-ers across the globe.

“The show is meant to be about three characters who see themselves as main characters in a TV show about themselves,” Reich explains. “And they’ve grown up watching all of this stuff about how being in your 20s in a big city is mean to look, and they’re failing to do it.”

Ethan is looking for love in all the wrong places while refusing to look for a job; Abi is doing everything to convince herself to stay in an unfulfilling relationship out of longing for a traditional life; and Sam is a struggling writer who finds herself sharing an apartment — and a lover — with her ex. In short, adulthood isn’t what they thought it would be.

“It’s this pseudo intellectual, kind of self-aggrandizing thing of, this has to be romantic in some way,” Reich says. “It’s people living for the plot, and it’s like, there is no plot, sweetheart. This is your real life.”

Was “It Get Worse” based on Reich’s real life? Yes and no.

“My friends find it funny when I say it’s not, because they’re like, it obviously is. But it’s not true events,” Reich says. Ethan, Abi and Sam aren’t based on real people, but are instead “sort of different versions of me,” he adds. As for Ethan’s love life: “That’s based off like, 50 people — an amalgamation of some of the most inaccessible kind of bisexual men that I’ve thrown myself at in the most desperate ways. All of whom I’m still friends with.”

Beyond the three main characters, “It Gets Worse” also features an eclectic ensemble with some of the most impressive cameos in recent TV memory: There’s Andrew Scott as a hot therapist, bestselling author Zadie Smith as the show’s narrator and voice of reason, artist BabyMorocco as a douchey DJ, “Chicken Shop Date” host Amelia Dimoldenberg as an annoyingly nice it-girl and “Inbetweeners” star Blake Harrison as a quirky lodger Ethan’s mom takes in. Reich even recruited “Girls” creator Lena Dunham to play the Millennial girlboss at Abi’s office, who has become — in a plot twist 13-year-old him would not believe — a mentor of sorts.

The two met after Dunham watched a recording of Reich’s breakout Edinburgh Fringe Festival comedy show “Literally Who Cares?!” in 2022 — before it was picked up for HBO Max. “I get a call being like, ‘Lena Dunham’s written a part for you,'” Reich recalls. “I literally fell to the floor. I couldn’t believe it.”

That part was in “Too Much,” Dunham’s return to TV nearly a decade after “Girls” and love letter to her new life in London. Reich played Boss Gibbons, the painfully Gen-Z co-worker of Megan Stalter’s expat Jessica, in his first-ever screen acting role. “The first time I met her, I was so nervous — two seconds in, I’m screaming laughing,” he says of Dunham. “She’s just the easiest person to be around, and that whole thing was so fun.”

Naturally, Dunham gave Reich notes on the “It Gets Worse” pilot, and to his surprise, offered to guest star. “She went, ‘Oh, and I’d love to be in it if you want me to be,'” he says. “I was like, ‘What are you talking about?! Do I want you to be in it? Uh, yeah. I’m gonna write a part now .'”

Similar to “Girls,” “It Gets Worse” doesn’t shy away from sex. In fact, there’s an entire storyline based around a sex party gone wrong. But Reich insists he’s not trying to make a “conscious political statement” about sex on screen, despite reports that Gen Z could do without it.

“I just think sex is funny,” he says. “It felt to me like there was an era of very clean, sort of idealized sex scenes; almost educational on the one hand, or so eroticized that it becomes not hot on the other hand. Both of those things are great — it’s not, in my experience, how people have sex.”

Now that the series is premiering in America, Reich is anxious to see if it will be New York City stand-up all over again. (Judging by Variety ‘s glowing review , it won’t.) “There is some kind of significant cultural difference in what people find funny intuitively, so that will be interesting,” he says.

But Reich is hopeful that “It Gets Worse” will get a chance for a second season — he has “loads of ideas” — just so Ethan and his friends can see how much worse it can actually get.

“No one’s gonna make it! It’s in the fucking title,” he says with a cackle. “People going, ‘Aw, do they end up together?’ Bitch, read the title of the show. No one gets what they want ever.”

However, “The worst it could get is if it gets canceled, of course,” he adds, turning slightly serious. “But it was fun while it lasted. There’s a little bit of a badge of honor, I think, for a canceled after one season show. Kind of a cult classic.”

He’s also eyeing film in the future — maybe a rom-com, though he isn’t picky. “I’d love to do anything. Please, God,” he says. “If this is my job for the rest of my life, I’ll be the luckiest boy in the world.”

Title: Macklemore Accuses Madison Square Garden and Eight Other Arenas of Banning His ‘Free Palestine’ Tour
Main Body Text:
Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.

The rapper, who recently had dates in Dublin, Paris and London at the end of October, took to Instagram on Nov. 6 to say that he has been turned down by American venues, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, New Jersey’s Prudential Center, Brooklyn’s Barclays Center, Long Island’s UBS Arena, L.A.’s Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year,” he said in the Instagram post. “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table. The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

“In over 20 years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” he also wrote. “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.”

“We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending,” he later wrote. “Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow?”

Macklemore ended his post with, “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE!”

A spokesperson for MSG Entertainment responded to Macklemore’s claims in a statement to Variety : “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act.”

In September, Macklemore was fired from Ed Sheeran’s “Loop” tour over pro-Palestine comments he made during his opening set at MetLife Stadium. All of the tour’s other openers and Sheeran’s own backing band ended up quitting the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.

Variety has reached out to the nine arenas Macklemore mentioned for comment.

Title: Marilyn Monroe Retrospective at Torino to Portray Her as a ‘Female Marlon Brando’: ‘She Was So Profound’
Main Body Text:
Torino Film Festival marks Marilyn Monroe's centenary with wide-ranging retrospective

The dust had barely settled on last year’s Torino Film Festival when artistic director Giulio Base began plotting his next move.

2026 would mark the centenary of Marilyn Monroe ’s birth, and Base was determined not to be beaten to it. “I really wanted to be the first to announce a retrospective,” he says. “I knew this would be the anniversary year, and I knew others might be thinking the same.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The gambit paid off twice over. Announced just before the 2025 festival closed, the showcase staked Torino’s claim and gave Base’s team a focal point around which to build the new program.

This year’s 24-film lineup stretches well beyond Monroe’s own filmography. Classics like “The Seven Year Itch,” “How to Marry a Millionaire” and “Some Like It Hot” sit alongside revisionist takes such as Andrew Dominik’s “Blonde” and Pier Paolo Pasolini and Giovanni Guareschi’s documentary “La Rabbia” because the star’s relatively brief career simply didn’t offer enough leading roles to fill the schedule.

“Screening a movie where she has only a scene that isn’t even relevant would be a pity,” Base says. “So we decided to understand her complete legend, including the movies that celebrate her, or research her life, her problems, her traumas, her faults and her dreams.”

The program also traces her influence across the six decades since her death, finding echoes in films by guests of honor Luc Besson (“Dogman”) and Mira Sorvino (“Norma Jean & Marilyn”). Wherever the team looked, well, there she was, sharing her platinum-blond ‘do with honoree Pamela Anderson and casting new light on Roland Joffé’s “November 1963,” this year’s festival opener.

“In one sequence they go to a nightclub and there’s a Marilyn impersonator singing,” Base says of the film, which stars another Torino honoree, John Travolta . “I was almost screaming in the screening room. That’s such a great connection, helping our program look like a complete piece and not just a mosaic.”

Beyond the simple pleasure of great films on the big screen, Base sees Monroe’s ubiquity as a way to advance a broader effort to democratize the festival.

“When I started as director, our festival was known as prestigious but niche,” he explains. “But as a moviegoer, I think stars make everybody feel at home. Big stars like [previous retrospective subjects] Marlon Brando and Paul Newman make people approach the festival without feeling out of place. They welcome those beyond the inner circle, those who don’t know about Korean cinema of the 1940s or the history of movies. So it’s important to have an icon, a symbol, a totem, that makes us feel we’re all equal.”

Unlike Newman or Brando, Monroe never reached old age, and her legend was shaped in no small part by her untimely death. Base has therefore designed the retrospective to work on two levels: challenging those with limited or preconceived notions of Monroe, while offering newcomers a chance to discover her work.

“I always remember Lee Strasberg, that great master who taught some of the greatest actors in the world, saying that Marilyn Monroe was the female Marlon Brando,” he says. “She was so profound, and so literate. She was a great reader whose poetry, notes and diaries reveal a deep intellectual, adept at playing the ditz for the heavy fun of those of us who bought in. So I hope the new generations will discover the great actress beyond the big icon.”

Base is unlikely to announce next year’s tribute quite so early, as the 1927 birth cohort offers a less obvious marquee draw (Sidney Poitier and Peter Falk are certainly worthy of consideration; Roger Moore and Carl “Alfalfa” Switzer, perhaps less so).

Instead, he hints at plans for a more distant anniversary. “I have ideas for 2027 already, but I won’t say anything now,” he says. “It’s too soon, and it’s not so simple, like with Marilyn.”

Title: Meghan Markle’s Father Arrested Over Allegations He Possessed Child Sex Abuse Images
Main Body Text:
Meghan Markle ‘s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been arrested over allegations he possessed child sex abuse images.

The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida on Friday in connection with allegations that emerged last month , as the Daily Mail first reported and CBS News confirmed.

“A Florida man was arrested today on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades,” the U.S. Department of Justice said in a statement. “Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, of Lakeland, Florida, is charged with one count of possession of child pornography.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

A DOJ press release said that the FBI searched the storage units, which Markle Sr. had kept since 2008, and “seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected CSAM.” The affidavit describes several images, two of which “depict an adult man – whom a witness identified as Markle – with a nude prepubescent girl. The third image depicts a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines,” the release continued.

Markle Sr. is expected to appear in court in Tampa, Florida on Friday.

Last month, a report in The Sun claimed that child sex abuse images had allegedly been found in his former home in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. Markle Sr. vehemently denied the allegations to the Daily Mail, calling them “a bunch of lies” and adding: “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

In a statement at the time, the Duchess of Sussex said she was “deeply distressed” at the news. She claimed that in 2018, a letter about her father was sent to the Metropolitan Police and its Royalty and Specialist Protection unit and was “subsequently shared” with her.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

The Metropolitan Police said at the time that they were “undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm” that a letter had been passed from their officers to Meghan. It is understood that the Met has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle Sr.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he failed to walk her down the aisle at her wedding. She was escorted by King Charles instead. Thomas Markle has never met her and Prince Harry ’s two children. Last year, she sent a letter to him while he was in the hospital getting his left lower leg amputated due to a blood clot.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan concluded.

The FBI also issued a statement last month saying that they were “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”

Representatives for Meghan Markle did not immediately respond to Variety ’s request for comment on Markle Sr.’s arrest. Variety has also attempted to contact Markle Sr. for comment.

Title: Melania Trump Series Sets Amazon Release Date
Main Body Text:
Amazon Prime Video will release its two-part Melania Trump docuseries on Nov. 20.

The previously announced series, which will include “content never before shared with the public,” is split between two episodes: “Family & Trust,” which follows Trump as she prepares to become the First Lady, and “Pride & Honor,” which takes place moments after the inauguration.

The docuseries follows the theatrical release of “Melania” on Jan. 30 and the film’s streaming release on March 9. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

While a press release from Amazon touts “the historic success of ‘Melania, The Film,'” the movie lost tens of millions of dollars. It is true that the film outperformed expectations for a documentary at the box office, garnering $16.6 million worldwide, but considering Amazon paid a whopping $40 million for the rights to “Melania” — plus a $35 million marketing spend — the studio failed to recoup its investment theatrically.

“Melania” is directed by Brett Ratner and executive produced by Trump herself alongside Marc Beckman. Ratner produces with Fernando Sulichin, as well as Muse Films, New Element Media and RatPac Entertainment.

Variety ‘s chief film critic Owen Gleiberman hated “Melania, The Film,” calling it a “cheeseball infomercial of staggering inertia.”

“It’s a ‘portrait’ of the First Lady of the United States, but it’s so orchestrated and airbrushed and stage-managed that it barely rises to the level of a shameless infomercial,” he wrote in his review . “Is it cheesy? At moments, but mostly it’s inert. It feels like it’s been stitched together out of the most innocuous outtakes from a reality show. There’s no drama to it. It should have been called ‘Day of the Living Tradwife.'”

Title: Natalia Dyer, Elijah Wood to Join John Cusack and Samuel L. Jackson in ‘1408’ Sequel From Director Mikael Håfström (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
Natalia Dyer and Elijah Wood are set to join original cast members Samuel L. Jackson and John Cusack , who are currently negotiating the terms of their return, in a sequel to the 2007 supernatural horror film “1408,” Variety can reveal exclusively. Mikael Håfström, who directed the first film, returns to helm the sequel, which he co-wrote with Mark Verheiden.

While Jackson and Cusack will reprise their original roles, they will be secondary characters in the sequel, according to a source familiar with the project. Dyer will star in the film, and Wood will play a supporting role. Details about their characters remain under wraps. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Lorenzo di Bonaventura, Bluestone Entertainment’s Richard Saperstein, Spyglass Media Group and Frank Mayor serve as producers. Bluestone Entertainment and FilmNation Entertainment are co-financing, with FilmNation representing the international distribution rights, co-representing domestic rights with WME Independent and introducing it to buyers at AFM next week. John Papsidera (“The Odyssey”) serves as casting director. Production is currently slated to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

Based on Stephen King’s 1999 short story of the same name, “1408” follows author Michael Enslin, played by Cusack, who, as part of his new book on haunted hotels, investigates legends of mysterious and violent deaths behind door 1408 at the Dolphin Hotel in New York City. Jackson co-stars as Gerald Olin, the Dolphin Hotel’s manager. Plot details for the sequel have not been disclosed.

“1408,” released by MGM, was a cult hit in 2007, grossing $132 million worldwide against a slim budget of just $25 million. Cusack has gone on record saying it would be the only film he’d ever do a sequel for, telling People in 2025, “I was lucky that I never had the desire, or no one asked me to do any sequels. There’s one that I think would be interesting to do, which would be ‘1408.’ Just because … I think today, you know, most movies suck.”

Dyer rose to global recognition through her breakout role as Nancy Wheeler in Netflix’s marquee series “Stranger Things.” She is currently in production on HBO’s true-crime limited series, “The Trial of Louise Woodward.” She also has Oran Zegman’s rom-com “Goodbye Girl,” starring Kiernan Shipka and Cole Sprouse, on the horizon. Her previous credits include the coming-of-age comedy film, “Yes, God, Yes,” from writer-director Karen Maine.

“Lord of the Rings” icon Wood has become a horror genre regular, recently appearing in “Ready or Not 2: Here I Come,” “The Toxic Avenger” and Osgood Perkins’ “The Monkey.” It was recently revealed that Wood will return to Middle-earth as Frodo Baggins in Andy Serkis’ “LOTR” sequel “The Hunt for Gollum.” Wood is also joining the cast of Netflix’s “The Gentlemen” for Season 3.

Cusack, best known for roles in “Say Anything,” “High Fidelity” and “Being John Malkovich,” was a staple leading man throughout the ‘90s and early 2000s, but has mostly stayed out of the spotlight in recent years. His last big-screen credits were for the 2025 thriller “Fog of War” and a pair of foreign films: “Detective Chinatown 1900” and “Decoded.”

Jackson, the star of “Pulp Fiction,” “Avengers” and “The Hateful Eight,” likewise rose to stardom in the ’90s and has been all over the big screen lately. His most recent film roles were “The Beast,” which hit theaters on Oct. 9, and “Just Play Dead.” His upcoming projects include J.J. Abrams’s “The Great Beyond,” “The Incredibles 3” and “Avengers: Secret Wars.”

Dyer is represented by Circle Management + Production, CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Wood is represented by Linden Entertainment, Gersh and Meyer & Downs. Cusack is represented by Link Entertainment, Wolf Kasteler Public Relations and Ziffren Brittenham. Jackson is represented by Anonymous Content, CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein.

Title: Netflix Alum Emily Feingold Joins Disney as Executive VP of Communications
Main Body Text:
Mouse stalwart David Jefferson takes early retirement after 15 years in corporate PR department

Netflix alum Emily Feingold has joined the Walt Disney Co. as executive VP of communications, where she will steer media relations, financial and technology communications as well as enterprise editorial, executive and brand messaging.

Feingold’s move to Disney in a senior communications role comes five months after she left Netflix following a nine-year tenure with the streaming giant. Feingold steps into the role held by David Jefferson, who has taken the company’s voluntary early retirement offer after spending the past 15 years as a senior Disney corporate communications executive. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Feingold reports to Paul Roeder, who ascended to senior executive VP and chief communications office in March after Josh D’Amaro was tapped as the Mouse House’s new CEO. Feingold is respected as a straight-shooter from her years in the trenches during Netflix’s stunning rise.

“Emily is one of the best in the business,” Roeder said. “She combines sharp instincts, broad experience and the trust and respect of colleagues and journalists alike. She’s led communications through some of the most transformative moments in our industry, and she’ll be a tremendous asset as we head into an exciting chapter for Disney.”

Before joining Netflix, Feingold served as senior VP of corporate strategy and communications at private investment firm Andell Inc. She served as VP of corporate communications for fashion giant Ralph Lauren. Feingold began her career at the White House.

Jefferson will remain on board during the transition period through the end of the month. He first joined Disney’s PR ranks in 2009 when he signed on with Walt Disney Parks and Resorts. He left the Mouse at end of 2010 but returned in January 2013 in a corporate communications role. He was most recently upped to exec VP of corporate communications in March 2025.

Before Disney, Jefferson had a 14-year run at the Wall Street Journal in a variety of roles, including deputy Los Angeles bureau chief. He also worked as a top editor at Newsweek for eight years, followed later by another stint at Newsweek and the Daily Beast after he left Disney in 2010.

“David has been a trusted voice and steady hand for Disney through some of the most consequential moments in our history,” Roeder said. “I’ve known him since his days as a reporter, and I’m deeply grateful for his counsel, his friendship and everything he’s done for this company. I wish him every success in what comes next.”

Title: Nick Cave Returning to North America for 25-Date ‘Evening of Talk and Music’ in Spring
Main Body Text:
Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

Eight years after touring with a combination of audience Q&As and solo music, Nick Cave will return to North America with “Conversations With Nick Cave: An Evening of Talk and Music,” a followup to his 2019 tour of the same name. This followup is set to run for 25 dates in the U.S. and Canada in the spring.

The shows begin April 9, 2027 at Vancouver’s Queen Elizabeth Theatre and wrap up May 21 at New Orleans’ Saenger Theatre. In the six weeks in-between, Cave has two-night stands booked at L.A.’s Orpheum (April 20-21), Brooklyn’s Kings Theatre (May 7-8) San Francisco’s Orpheum (April 16-17), Seattle’s 5th Ave. Theatre (April 13-14), Toronto’s Massey Hall (April 29-30) and Boston’s Boch Center Schubert Theatre (May 4-5). Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Single appearances are on the lineup for Portland, Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Montreal, Philadelphia, Washington, D.C., Asheville and Atlanta, in addition to the Vancouver and New Orleans bookends. (Scroll down for the full list of appearances.)

The shows are being described as “a mixture of unvetted audience questions and intimate performances of Cave’s extensive catalog at the piano.”

Said Cave in a statement, “Years ago, in a peculiar state of mind, I traveled across the U.S., stepped onto stages in different cities, and fielded questions from the audience. It was a strange, almost desperate idea, but those nights became deeply healing for me. I hope the audience felt the same.

“Eight years have passed,” he continued. “The Red Hand Files have grown in reach and stature; the topics of conversation have broadened, and it feels like the right time to return to America, a different America from eight years ago, and bring the ‘Conversations…’ show back. I’ll have my piano with me, play some songs, and answer questions. What could possibly go wrong?”

Title: Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘Take Me Home (4 Christmas)’ Effusively Endorsed by Writer of the Waitresses’ ‘Christmas Wrapping,’ Who Praises Her for Picking Up the ‘Vibe’ 45 Years Later
Main Body Text:
Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

Olivia Rodrigo ‘s first holiday single, “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” earned plenty of plaudits upon coming out of the gate late Thursday night — none greater than that offered by Chris Butler , the writer of the Waitresses ‘ classic 1981 song “Christmas Wrapping,” who said he’d been offered a sneak peek two months ago by Rodrigo.

The new tune is a Christmas rock banger, the likes of which are rarely heard nowadays. While there is no notable compositional or lyrically similarity between “Take Me Home” and “Christmas Wrapping,” the new song has much the same loose, spry and irreverently romantic spirit about it, and some fans of Christmas music were quick to sense Rodrigo’s song being in the spiritual lineage of the Waitresses’, if nothing else. Butler stepped up to say he was happy to pass on the torch, and in fact, had done so long before anyone in the general public was aware of the track. Related Stories Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism? Taylor Swift’s Canceled Vienna Concerts Due to Thwarted Terrorist Plot to Be Subject of Documentary

“Her song was/is great. It’s going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas #1 contest they have every year in the UK,” Butler enthused on his Facebook page. “I think it’s a fantasticbangersmash, and if it has the same upbeat vibe as ‘CW,’ well…how cool is that? I’m a fan, and I wish her monster success with it. Thanks, Olivia, for the chance to connect.”

Butler was gently snapping back at some Rodrigo antagonists on social media who claimed that the two songs sound too similar. “Thank you for all the comparisons to ‘Christmas Wrapping’,” he wrote in response to one commenter. “The vibe is there, but no plagiarism — and this is from the guy who wrote ‘CW.’ LOVE O.R., too. Happy holidays.”

It may be amusing to some to learn that Butler, 77, had not heard of Rodrigo before getting her note, and, once apprised of who it was, remained in disbelief that it really came from her.

Butler’s original Facebook message:

BACKSTORY: About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be “Olivia Rodrigo”. It was filled w/ Waitresses gush, and just had to be fake. Said she’d written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it. ????? I didn’t know who OR was, so I did a deep dig. Wow…what a career. So, I wrote back:

“Um… Er… Well. If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering. They’re really sweet and flattering…even if you AREN’T you. If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you. I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them. I like that you’re insisting on/demanding that you be recognized as a songwriter. I like that you have women in your band. I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you “got” my songwriting, and that you like our band. I like that you were smart enough to hold on to your masters when you signed your deal. I like that you are you, and will growgrowgrow. …and I would be honored to hear your Christmas song. Really. Best/CB” …Then she invited Beth and I to her Daisy Chain Festival in LA. Too short notice, but then I got texts from her minder at her label. OR’s 86 show/6 month tour was landing in Columbus, and Ms. Minder repeatedly said “She wants to meet you”. So, Beth & I did meet her after the show. After just killing it for two+ hours…. A delight.

After the BBC posted a story about his message, Butler continued to shower further praise on Rodrigo, writing, “Kudos to Olivia Rodrigo for doing the right thing. Respect, Fan Boy gush, and wishing that her song is a monster smash.”

“Christmas Wrapping” was written solely by Butler for the group, which was one of the best to come out of the new wave era, and sung by frontwoman Patty Donahue. It was only a cult for song for years after its initial issue 45 years ago — and at first paled in popularity in comparison to their earliest hit, “I Know What Boys Like,” not to mention their “Square Pegs” TV Theme. But in recent years it has come to be as much of a standard on Christmas playlists as smashes from much bigger pop artists of the same era, like Wham!’s “Last Christmas.” The group went separate ways later in the 1980s, and Donahue died of lung cancer in 1996.

Title: Over 20 Years, ‘Kung Fu Deadly’ Filmmakers Made a Supernatural Action Comedy That Blended ‘80s Favorites: ‘To Make it Coherent Felt Like a Really Fun Challenge’
Main Body Text:
Some genre movies are stripped-back exercises: lean, mean and to the point. Some films, like “ Kung Fu Deadly ,” take the opposite approach, dipping into multiple genres in a sumptuous visual feast.

“Deadly” follows Danny and Frank (Steven He and Michael Tient), two hapless exterminators in Dublin, as they are called upon to combat a supernatural evil. Audiences at genre festivals from Austin’s Fantastic Fest to Spain’s Sitges Film Festival have received it warmly, and it will have a wider distribution plan this spring. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Director Fergal Costello says he and cinematographer Shing-Fung Cheung thought about the visual style of this fantastical slacker tale as “primary color that’s covered in grime.”

“I just thought that was a visual language that reflected Danny’s journey,” the director says. “He has so much depth, color and heroism inside him — if he just believed in himself and wiped the grime off, wiped off the self-doubt. We wanted the movie to feel that, while being very colorful, because I frankly don’t think movies are colorful enough at the moment. Life is there and bursting out through the frame — you just have to look for it.”

Yet getting to that point of production was decades in the making. Writer Paddy McDonald says “Deadly” originally developed alongside fellow Irish writer Paul Markey and was born from their love of martial arts movies, from Shaw Brothers classics to Jackie Chan blockbusters.

“It’s been a bit of a labor of love for quite a long time,” McDonald says. “It was an idea I came across with him 20 years ago. It’s been bouncing around my life a little bit since then, but properly started developing it in 2011. I was living in Australia at the time. There’ve been a few different iterations of it and many, many drafts. I was living away from Ireland and moved back a couple of years ago and did a page one rewrite, bringing it back home. That’s when it started to make the most sense and had its original Irish voice.”

Once it came to filming, finding the right chemistry between the two central characters was central — and could help ground all of the disparate genres the film plays with.

“If we root the film in the relationship with the two boys together, Danny and Frank, then I think we can get away with all the other tones and not feel like they’re clashing together,” Costello says. “If we experience this clash happening through their eyes as they come into the movie and become more than just those lovable losers, the monsters and the magic and the comedy and the horror stuff will all work. Making the relationship between the two boys work was critical.”

Just as Danny and Frank found themselves trying to clean up supernatural entities, Costello and McDonald brought a parallel ethos to the set, where they mounted an eco-friendly production. In fact, it was Ireland’s first to be powered by green hydrogen fuel cells, versus diesel. It’s a milestone that the team is passionate about advocating for, as they can demonstrate the great results of environmentally friendly productions.

“While we were shooting there, we were able to power the entire thing with green hydrogen,” McDonald says. “The differences are how silent it is, how clean it is, how you can control these things. It’s like the difference between a diesel car and an electric car. You can turn it on remotely, you can turn it off remotely. There’s also data available to a production to understand the actual amount of energy that’s actually required. Once we got it set up and running, it was seamless. Whilst they’re a bit anxious about it at the beginning, I ended up loving it because it was so dependable, it was so quiet, it was so clean. It was a really positive experience.”

Much like taking the environmental challenge head-on, Costello says “Kung Fu Deadly” was a complex journey he couldn’t say no to.

“The idea of all those tones clashing together and trying to make it coherent felt like a really fun challenge, to be honest,” he says. “It wasn’t something I was very fearful of. It was something I wanted to jump at.”

Title: Pamela Abdy Delivers Fiery Speech After Warner Bros. Exit: ‘It Is Getting Harder, Not Easier, to Be a Woman in the Business’
Main Body Text:
A month after her departure from Warner Bros. was announced, Pamela Abdy made her first industry appearance Thursday night at the Women in Film Honors at Los Angeles’ Beverly Hilton.

The event marked a full-circle moment of sorts. On the morning of Oct. 1, Abdy was announced as WIF’s inaugural Vanguard Award recipient. Then, she was serving as co-chair and CEO of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group with her longtime producing partner Michael DeLuca. But later that night, Abdy and DeLuca learned that they would not usher the film studio into its next chapter amid the Skydance merger. Just over a month later, Abdy was ready to talk about it. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

During the gala, Abdy delivered a fiery 15-minute address that held the ballroom at rapt attention. The thesis of her remarks: after 31 years in Hollywood, she was no longer worried about being called “difficult” if she laid bare the realities of being a woman in the film business; instead, Abdy spoke her truth about the “pure unadulterated rage” she’s been feeling about the state of the business and how she’s using that as “fuel” for change.

But before she took the stage, Abdy walked the red carpet and updated the press on what she’d been up to in recent weeks.

“Right now, I’m taking a break and chilling,” Abdy told Variety ‘s Marc Malkin. “I got to go see every single one of my daughter’s volleyball games, without being interrupted. So that’s what I’m doing right now.”

When Malkin asked her about the swirling rumors about her next stop, including the idea that she and De Luca could fill the open film head job at Netflix, Abdy said, “When I decide what I’m doing, I promise I will tell everyone. But honestly, it’s an interesting time to be able to take a break, and really decide what I want.

“I know what happiness is when I’m working with filmmakers, and wherever and whatever I end up doing, that’s my goal is to continue to work with the best storytellers out there,” Abdy said.

When Malkin asked if she thinks the new combined company can reach its goal of releasing 30 movies a year, Abdy replied, “I don’t know. I’m not there. I hope they do.”

A month after her departure from Warner Bros. was announced, Pamela Abdy made her first industry appearance Thursday night at the Women in Film Honors, where she described what she's focusing on. “Right now, I’m taking a break and chilling,” she told Variety on the red carpet.… pic.twitter.com/p4YOj31oHv

If Abdy’s replies seem a little vague, that was, perhaps, by design. She was saving her energy for the barnburner of a speech she was preparing to deliver a couple hours later.

WIF Honors also saluted Adria Arjona with the WIF Max Mara Face of the Future Award; “Josephine” filmmaker Beth de Araújo and star Gemma Chan (in absentia) with the Crystal Award for Advocacy in Film; “Ted Lasso” star Hannah Waddingham with the Crystal Award for Advocacy in TV; and Salma Hayek Pinault with the Jane Fonda Humanitarian Award, presented by Fonda. The Vanguard Award was slated for the end of the program, so just after 9 p.m., Nancy Meyers took the stage to present the WIF prize to Abdy.

“I’ve learned over my many years here in Hollywood, behind every great woman, you will generally find another great woman,” Meyers said before reading out a list of women filmmakers whom Abdy has championed over the years, including herself. (Abdy and DeLuca greenlit Meyers’ next movie “Paris Paramount” at Warner Bros.)

“I’ve been making movies for 46 years, and I’ve worked with quite a few of the great women studio heads, and I’ll tell you… they’re nothing like the guys,” Meyers added.

“What’s different about them is that they approach the job in a unique way: They treat you like a friend, and a friend they want to support, and a friend they want to go to bat for,” she explained. “They’re very smart about filmmaking. They’re tuned into the process. They’re open, and they’re trusting. They want to tell stories about women, but most importantly, they all love movies. It’s that simple. And Pam is very much a significant part of that rarefied breed.”

Indeed, the WIF prize recognizes the breadth of Abdy’s career beyond Warner Bros., where she oversaw blockbusters and award darlings including “One Battle After Another,” “Sinners,” “Barbie,” “Weapons” and “Dune: Part Two.” Last year, Warner Bros. tied the all-time studio record with 11 Academy Awards from an industry-leading 30 nominations. (That said, not all of the Abdy and DeLuca’s big-budget swings paid off, with “The Bride!” and “Digger” as two recent financial misfires.) But this particular evening wasn’t about balancing box office budgets — in fact, Abdy later lamented the deficiencies of traditional box office tracking methods — it was a moment to celebrate the battles Abdy had won in the name of creatives.

Before she took the stage, a slew of A-listers appeared in a clip to congratulate her. Sandra Bullock kicked off the reel, playfully alluding to Abdy’s change in employment status. “Just stay really chill. Just say thank you and, you know, get out of there quickly,” the “Practical Magic” star joked, before someone off camera reminded her Abdy was being recognized by Women in Film. “Forget everything I just said,” Bullock pivoted. “Say everything you want to say. Toot your own horn.”

Joining Bullock for the video salute were her “Practical Magic” co-star Nicole Kidman; “Digger” star Tom Cruise, director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and producer Mary Parent; “Sinners” filmmaker Ryan Coogler and star Michael B. Jordan; “Barbie,” “Wuthering Heights” and “Oceans” producer/star Margot Robbie; “Queen & Slim” filmmaker Melina Matsoukas; and “Garden State” filmmaker Zach Braff, among others. Finally, it was time for Abdy to take the stage, and she was welcomed by a standing ovation from the well-heeled crowd — made up mostly of women and a few male allies.

Abdy kicked off her remarks by digging into the definition of the term vanguard. “I came across a few meanings that stood out to me, but two in particular spoke to my experience working in Hollywood,” she began. “The first, also known as the ‘advance guard,’ is to lead an advancing military formation, securing ground ahead of the main force. It also means a leader who brings new ideas, political movements, or art. Both definitions spoke to me because they exemplify in one word how I approach my professional life. I see my role as needing to look 10 steps ahead and forming a formidable team as we head into battle, while also creating space for new voices.”

Over the years, Abdy said, she’s been in the trenches with some of the greatest filmmakers of all time — “both men and women” — all with one mission in mind: “To tell stories, to reach into people’s minds and pull at their hearts, to make people laugh and cry and see the world through someone else’s eyes; to ask the audience to experience ideas and issues that may feel challenging but will also lead to valuable conversations and debate.” She added, defiantly: “We also have to do this under the microscope of a media ecosystem that has largely abandoned analysis and fact for the trap of clickbait based in rumor.”

Here, Abdy took a moment to thank the long list of women directors she’s worked with over the years, including Meyers, Kasi Lemmons, Karyn Kusama, Greta Gerwig, Emerald Fennell, Sarah Polley, Matsoukas, A.V. Rockwell, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Olivia Wilde, Zoë Kravitz and more. “You are all powerful. You have a lot to say, so please keep sharing your stories and do it fearlessly and loudly,” she said.

She also thanked the women producers and executives she’s learned from over the years, like Stacey Sher, Sherry Lansing, Donna Langley, Dede Gardner, and more. “My gratitude for these women has only grown over the years,” Abdy said, really starting to hit her stride. “But lately, other feelings and one in particular have risen to the surface with undeniable ferocity: and that feeling is pure, unadulterated rage.”

“Rage for these women, rage for me, and even more rage for the entire generation of women who deserve to have their potential recognized and elevated,” Abdy continued as the crowd cheered their approval. “Rage at how women are under attack everywhere. Rage at how our health and our well-being always seem to come second to how we show up in a room. And here’s the problem: as a leader who happens to be a woman, I am supposed to sublimate this rage, and you know what happens when they tell you to tamp down a fever? Sometimes it just burns hotter.”

Over the course of her career, Abdy recalled being called “difficult,” “emotional” and “combative.” She’s been told to “put on [her] big boy pants” and to “smile more.” While those are microaggressions women everywhere and in every industry can relate to, Abdy shared more examples specific to the movie business.

“I’ve been told movies starring women and movies directed by women don’t make as much money. That the audience is limited. That everyone gets nervous when our sisters lead a movie because traditional tracking suggests men won’t show up,” she said. “Well, if this is really a reality — and I’m really not sure anymore that tracking effectively depicts reality — I say, why is it given that women will show up for the quote-unquote male movies, bringing their friends, kids, partners, parents, and siblings to experience the wonders of the big screen, and men will not do the same for female-driven stories?”

Abdy, for one, would like to see that gender trope “obliterated,” and she’s hopeful that “new generations of moviegoers will step outside these boxes and celebrate filmmakers of every gender, race, and age.” That way, the industry can stop “thinking that tracking is somehow a measure of success or a roadmap to what stories we should tell,” she said.

Not to mention the fact that male directors are quick to show up for one another, but where’s that support for the women directors?” “They deserve your advocacy, too,” Abdy said.

Here, Abdy shared a hard truth. “It is getting harder, not easier, to be a woman in the business,” she said. “We tell ourselves because a few of us made it into these chairperson seats, we broke through; that we paved the way for the next generation. But I don’t think it’s true.”

Why not? “We still have the most powerful women in Hollywood list. The men don’t have a separate list; they are the list,” Abdy explained. “When Greta Gerwig made ‘Barbie,’ a movie that grossed over $1.4 billion, people consistently referred to her as a female director — not a director, a female director. … This industry has kept finding ways to put an asterisk next to a woman’s success, as if it’s exceptional for a woman, instead of just being exceptional.”

It’s these questions Abdy has been musing over lately: “What business are we leaving for future vanguards? Is it a healthy industry for the next generation of storytellers and executives to step into? One that allows women to enter with an open heart and mind without having to fight the fights we’re still fighting.”

Rather than letting her rage be destructive, Abdy is using these feelings as fuel. She sees it as “something that can burn bright, something that can be harnessed to fight on for what we think is right, what we believe in, and what we deserve.” She added: “It is incredibly heartening this week to see so many women elected on Tuesday. I truly, for the first time this week, have hope for the next generation.”

After thanking her industry partners (from Danny DeVito to DeLuca), friends and family for supporting her through her journey, Abdy closed out her passionate remarks with a final nugget of wisdom.

“I look out at this amazing, amazing collection of pioneers and positively incredible women, and I am struck by this personal truth,” Abdy said. “It has taken me 31 years in this business to speak in my own voice and to stop caring whether someone calls me ‘difficult.'”

“Because now, when I hear that, I say, ‘No, you’re wrong.’ If the definition of difficult is someone who is passionate about getting movies made, then I will just have to suffer the fools who don’t know the difference and keep fighting to do what I love,” she concluded. “I am so grateful and so blessed for this life I have and this career so far. I’m not done.”

Title: Paramount Network Orders 13 Original Episodes of Larry the Cable Guy-Hosted Clip Show ‘American Mayhem’ (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
“ American Mayhem ,” the new syndicated half-hour clip series hosted by Larry the Cable Guy , is getting a linear cable platform as well. Paramount Network has ordered 13 episodes of “American Mayhem” from producer V10 Entertainment .

The 13 episodes, which will launch Friday, Nov. 13, at 9 p.m. ET, will be new and original to Paramount Network. The deal is separate from the 52-episode syndicated version of “American Mayhem” distributed to stations by CBS Media Ventures. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Here’s the logline for “American Mayhem”: “With his signature heartland humor, Larry the Cable Guy guides viewers through a fast-paced collection of funny, unexpected and relatable moments captured across America. From backyard mishaps and weekend DIY disasters to pets stealing the spotlight and celebrations that don’t go as planned, ‘American Mayhem’ finds the humor in everyday life, with clips spanning small towns, ball fields, family gatherings and more.”

“‘American Mayhem’ reflects the humor and unpredictability of everyday life in an entertaining way,” said Laurel Weir, head of programming and acquisitions for Paramount Media Networks and chief research and insights officer for TV Media, in a statement. “Larry the Cable Guy is the perfect comedian to bring these moments to life, with his natural ability to connect with audiences. We’re excited to partner with V10 Entertainment to bring this new format to Paramount Network with a host whose voice and perspective make it distinctly his own.”

“American Mayhem” is executive produced by Larry The Cable Guy, Maggie Houlehan, Carter Skeath, Rick De Oliveira, Josh Vodnoy and John Stevens. The syndicated version of “American Mayhem” is cleared across major markets including WLNY New York, KCAL Los Angeles and WCIU Chicago.

“Larry doesn’t just make people laugh; he understands the people he’s making laugh, and that’s what makes him so uniquely suited for ‘American Mayhem,’” said V10 Entertainment president Carter Skeath in a statement. “The show embraces the funny, unpredictable, rough-and-tumble side of Americana that feels right at home on Paramount Network. It’s also another opportunity to build on a partnership we genuinely value with an incredible team at Skydance.”

Added Larry the Cable Guy, in a statement: “I watch a ton of the shows on Paramount Network and to see ‘Mayhem’ premiere on their platform is something I’m really excited about — nothing celebrates this country like watching somebody’s uncle fall through a lawn chair.”

Title: Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Russell Crowe Sci-Fi Thriller ‘Bluefly’ Adds ‘Beast’ Star Daniel MacPherson (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
Daniel MacPherson , who recently starred opposite Russell Crowe in “Beast,” has signed on for “ Bluefly ,” a science-fiction action thriller toplined by Crowe and Priyanka Chopra Jonas .

“Predators” filmmaker Nimród Antal is directing.
