Title: Russell Brand’s Marriage to Katy Perry Blocked From Being Mentioned by Prosecution in Rape Trial
Main Body Text:
Russell Brand ‘s marriage to Katy Perry was reportedly blocked from being mentioned in the prosecution’s opening arguments in his London rape and sexual assault trial following objections from the comedian’s legal team.

Brand, 51, was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, following a four-week trial. He was acquitted of three other charges. The comedian, who denied all allegations of non-consensual sexual activity, is scheduled to be sentenced on Monday. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

According to details of pre-trial proceedings made public after his conviction, prosecutors had planned to reference Brand’s relationship with Perry, whom he married in 2010. However, his defense successfully challenged the inclusion of the singer in the prosecution’s opening statement, arguing against introducing details of his personal life that were unrelated to the allegations.

“The prosecution recognise that matters post 2009 involving his relationship with Katy Perry may be sensitive, as may his previous faiths, and we are content to remove these from the opening,” lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC said in pre-trial submissions, according to a report from The Telegraph.

Perry was also reportedly not asked to provide a witness statement during the police investigation. Although her name was absent from the prosecution’s opening remarks, Brand himself referenced their marriage while testifying, describing the period as one in which he achieved “staggering fame.”

The former couple began dating in 2009. They married in a Hindu ceremony in Rajasthan, India, the following year, before separating in December 2011. Their divorce was finalized in 2012.

Brand’s defense also objected to the prosecution introducing evidence concerning his history of alcohol and drug addiction, arguing that none of the complainants had alleged he was under the influence during the incidents in question.

Testimony from Brand’s former assistant Helen Berger was also edited to exclude references to his treatment at a sex addiction clinic, although jurors were permitted to hear her describe his sexual behavior, including what she characterized as an “insane sexual appetite.”

Prosecutors additionally agreed to omit references to Brand’s earlier religious practices and his 2024 baptism. Brand has made his Christian faith a heightened focus of his public persona since the allegations against him emerged in 2023.

A representative for Perry did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment. Variety has also reached out to the Crown Prosecution Service for confirmation.

Title: Salon.com Shuts Down Cultural and Political Site After 31 Years
Main Body Text:
Salon.com , the website that became popular in the early days of the internet offering cultural commentary, progressive political analysis, lifestyle content and more, is shutting down, the company announced Thursday.

“When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing,” the editorial team wrote in a statement. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The San Francisco-based site was known for launching numerous writers’ careers and was a daily stop for many readers in the days before social media. Among the film critics that wrote for Salon were Stephanie Zacharek, Andrew O’Hehir and Charles Taylor. The site’s television writers and critics included Heather Havrilesky, Hanh Nguyen, Maureen Ryan and Melanie McFarland.

Salon joins later-arriving sites such as Buzzfeed and Gawker that found it difficult to monetize cultural and topical reporting for a general audience and eventually shut down.

“The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” the editors continued in their statement. “After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

“Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege,” the statement concluded.

Title: South International Series Festival to Launch 2027 Investors Week, Linking Producers With Private Capital
Main Body Text:
Organized with Mira Anta, the Cádiz forum will feature project pitches, investor meetings and discussions on audiovisual financing during South's spring edition

South International Series Festival will launch a new investment forum in Cádiz in 2027, bringing audiovisual producers and companies together with private financiers, Womack Group announced during this year’s edition.

Called South Investors Week , the event is scheduled for April 30-May 5, 2027, during South’s fifth edition. It is being organized with Mira Anta , an audiovisual investment fund promoted by Womack’s Mira Entertainment Capital and managed by Anta Asset Management. The dates mark South’s move from autumn to spring. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The program will feature project pitches, investment presentations, one-to-one meetings between producers and financiers, and discussions on funding and business models. Organizers said international firms specializing in audiovisual finance are expected to attend, although no participants have yet been named.

The forum is aimed at investment funds and financial institutions as well as production companies, platforms and audiovisual technology businesses. Companies will be able to present projects and expansion plans to potential financial and industrial partners.

Mira Anta Media Capital Fund I, launched in May and registered with Spain ’s CNMV financial regulator in June, has a fundraising target of €80 million ($90.1 million).

The fund plans to acquire stakes in audiovisual companies and provide financing for individual productions, including participatory loans tied to presales, distribution agreements and tax incentives, as well as gap financing. Its investment interests also cover virtual production and audiovisual technologies, including artificial intelligence applications.

“Spain’s audiovisual industry has talent, production capacity and an increasingly international reach. Yet it needs new financial tools and specialized capital to realize its full potential,” said José Carlos Conde, president of Mira Entertainment Capital and CEO of Womack Group.

“Investment should not be limited to financing productions; it can also contribute to the growth of companies, infrastructure, technologies and business models,” said Sergio Torras Soler, a financier involved in developing Mira Anta.

Womack produces South and is behind Mira Entertainment Capital, while Anta Asset Management is part of Corporación Financiera Azuaga.

In January, Mexico-based Punta Fina Studios announced a partnership with Womack Studios, the group’s audiovisual production arm, to establish a $47 million fund for developing series, telenovelas and films targeting Latin America and U.S. Hispanic audiences.

South’s fourth edition ran Oct. 30-Nov. 4 in Cádiz, combining series premieres, creative talks and industry events.

Title: Sweden’s Göteborg Film Festival to Debate the Fascination With Youth in a ‘Forever Young’ Focus
Main Body Text:
The festival’s first programming news for next year’s edition comes as Göteborg has also announced that Josef Kullengård will step down from his role as Head of industry after this year’s edition

Chief International Correspondent

Joshua Oppenheimer ’s “The Revolution Against Death,” Maria Martínez Bayona’s “The End of It” and William Greaves and David Greaves “ Once Upon a Time in Harlem ” will screen at a Gôteborg Film Festival 2027 Focus on the fascination of youth and the dream of immortality.

News of the Focus comes as Sweden’s Göteborg Festival, the biggest film-TV event in the Nordic countries, is set to celebrate its 50th anniversary at its 2027 edition, which runs Jan. 20-Feb. 6. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

From double Oscar-nominee Oppenheimer (“The Look of Silence,” “The Art of Killing”) and acquired by The New York Times’ Op-Docs platform, “The Revolution Against Death,” a 23-minute short, is set at an annual longevity conference, the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, observing its eccentric efforts to achieve immortality. Mubi will release alongside Op-Docs in December.

Starring Rebecca Hall , Gael García Bernal and Beanie Feldstein, sci-fi comedy-drama “The End of It” is set in a world where, at least for the rich, death is a choice. Claire, a 250-year-old artist played by Hall, seeks inspiration by choosing to die. Catalan Maria Martinez Bayona’s debut, “The End of It” bowed at the Cannes Festival’s Premiere section.

Described by Variety as “a documentary brimming with the wry and the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining,” “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” sees legendary 1920s Harlem Renaissance figures convene at a cocktail party in Duke Ellington’s townhouse in 1970. A “cultural time-capsule doc,” it is a portrait of a once-in-a lifetime party and the excitement of an all-consuming moment which become an epoch. “While you’re living it, it is the now,” remembers guest Bruce Richard Nugent, Variety notes in its review .

Past Göteborg Focus strands have been accompanied by a memorable event such as introducing a lie detector at the 2026 Göteborg, which focused on current concepts of truth.

Through film screenings and discussions, Focus: Forever Young will offer new perspectives on youth, aging, and society’s quest for immortality, the Göteborg Film Festival promised Thursday in a press release.

“We live in a time when everyone is expected to want to be young, no matter how old we actually are. But what happens when we’re never really allowed to grow old? With Focus: Forever Young we want to explore this era’s fixation with youth and ask questions about identity, life choices and what it means to become older,” said Göteborg Artistic Director Pia Lundberg,

She added: “As Göteborg Film Festival celebrates its 50th anniversary, Forever Young feels like a particularly suitable theme. We have grown older as a festival, but our curiosity about cinema and the world around us is as strong as it’s ever been. There’s something beautiful about that paradox: turning 50 by examining what it really means to be young,”

Josef Kullengård Steps Down From Göteborg to Join CPH:DOX

Göteborg’s first programming unveil for its 2027 edition came just two days after news that Josef Kullengård, Göteborg’s highly successful Head of Industry from 2022, will be joining Copenhagen’s CPH: Dox , one of Europe’s preeminent documentary festivals, as its new head of Industry & Training.

“On a personal level, my family and I have been wanting to move closer to friends and family in southern Scandinavia, so that has certainly been an important part of it. Professionally, I also feel ready for a new and exciting challenge,” Kullengård told Variety .

“I’ve always had a deep love for documentary cinema, particularly its ability to engage with social issues and the world around us, so the opportunity to join CPH:DOX felt incredibly meaningful,” he added.

Kullengård previously served over 2017-21 as Göteborg’s Industry Producer of the Nordic Film Market. He leaves Göteborg on a high-note. That was seen in a powerhouse 2026 edition which underscored how Göteborg under Kullengård, with Cecilie Edström heading up TV Drama Vision, has over the last decade consolidated as the Nordics’ premier film-TV market and industry forum.

This year’s edition saw a strong newsflow led by not only Europe’s superindies Banijay and Fremantle but also broadcaster networks New8 and Scandi Alliance and Charades and Dramanation, to name just a few. 2026’s event saw 2,600 accredited industry and press participants, 1,370 hailing from 47 countries attending the Nordic Film Market and TV Drama Vision, 50% up on 2023, as Göteborg remains a potential goldmine for tapping financing, even during ia bigger-picture Nordic market downturn.

Major talent – from Ruben Östlund to Erik Poppe, Dag Johan Haugerud, Milad Alami and Amanda Kernell – presented new projects. Two of the buzziest works in progress identified by Variety at the Nordic Film Market, Alex Schulman’s “Adult Supervision” and Eivind Landsvik’s “Low Expectations,” have now bowed, at Fantastic Fest and Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight respectively, ranking among the most exciting first features from Europe in 2026.

“I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved together in Göteborg over the past years. We’ve seen great development and growth, and I feel we’re at a point where the festival’s industry platform is in a really strong position. In many ways, that makes this feel like the right moment for someone new to take over, bring in new perspectives, and build on what we’ve accomplished,” Kullengård told Variety .

Upon the announcement of his CPH: DOX appointment, Kullengård’s Facebook account received 455 thumbs up and 157 comments, with people congratulating him on his new job and CPH:DOX for attracting him. Kullengård will stay on at Göteborg until the end of next year’s 50th anniversary edition.

“We would like to extend our warmest thanks to Josef Kullengård for his dedication, creativity and invaluable contributions over the years, and wish him all the best in his next chapter,” said Kristina Colliander, CEO of the Göteborg Film Festival.

Annika Pham contributed to this article

Title: Taiwan Audience Study Highlights Cross-Platform IP Opportunities as AI Raises New Risks for Content Industry
Main Body Text:
Taiwanese audiences are consuming entertainment across film, television, music, publishing and gaming, creating opportunities for cross-platform IP development, according to research presented by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei on Friday.

At the “Exclusive Insights Report: Taiwan Cross-Platform Audience Data × AI Application Evaluation” session, TAICCA research analyst Joy Lin presented findings from the agency’s annual cultural consumption survey and a 2026 cross-platform genre study incorporating Nielsen television ratings data and online questionnaires. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The annual survey, which collects approximately 2,000 valid responses each year, found that 96% of respondents watched audiovisual content in 2025, while 75% read published works and 75% played video games. Audiovisual content and music showed particularly strong audience overlap, with 90% of respondents engaging with both.

The separate cross-platform study surveyed 2,018 people aged 15 to 69. Among the 1,242 respondents who had watched Taiwanese audiovisual productions in the previous year, 40% had also watched Taiwanese screen adaptations.

Genre preferences revealed differences between local and imported content. Taiwanese productions were more closely associated with everyday life, family relationships and romance, while foreign productions showed greater strength in action, fantasy and suspense.

Romance emerged as a promising genre for cross-platform development, with the research identifying connections between romance, school-life stories, comics, popular music and mobile games. Among viewers of Taiwanese romantic dramas, 84% also watched foreign series, 63% watched foreign films and 58% watched foreign animation.

In the second presentation, TAICCA research analyst Chhoa Hiok-chong examined AI adoption in audiovisual production, highlighting potential cost savings alongside legal uncertainty and technical limitations.

Broader industry estimates cited in the presentation, rather than Taiwan-specific figures, placed AI adoption in post-production and visual effects at 70% to 85%, compared with 60% to 75% in pre-production and 15% to 25% in on-set production.

International examples included Netflix’s Argentine science-fiction series “The Eternaut” and South Korean entertainment company CJ ENM’s AI-assisted productions, illustrating potential savings in production costs and visual-effects workflows.

However, technical obstacles remain, including visual consistency across shots, camera control, narrative continuity and integration into established production pipelines.

Citing the Database of AI Litigation, the presentation identified 489 AI-related legal cases through August 2026, including 153 involving cultural and creative industries. The presentation also examined AI-related protections negotiated by Hollywood unions, including SAG-AFTRA, the Writers Guild of America (WGA), the Directors Guild of America (DGA) and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE), covering digital replicas, consent, compensation and creative control.

Consumer resistance presents another challenge. According to a November 2025 survey by entertainment research firm Luminate, 51% of U.S. respondents rejected fully synthetic virtual performers. A Japanese consumer survey published by English Hub and GRAS Group in September 2026 found that 44.7% would be less willing to purchase content once they knew it was AI-generated.

In South Korea, a survey published by Embrain Trend Monitor in January 2026 found that 81.6% supported advance disclosure of AI-generated content, while 80.3% favored mandatory AI labeling.

During the Q&A session, attendees questioned whether reported AI production savings adequately accounted for the upfront costs of adopting new workflows, including experimentation, revisions and trial-and-error processes. Others asked about the lack of Taiwan-specific production examples illustrating copyright disputes and legal responsibilities, given the presentation’s reliance on international cases.

Responding to questions about Taiwan’s regulatory framework, Chhoa pointed to the Ministry of Culture’s existing guidelines on generative AI in arts and culture.

Title: Taiwan Creative Content Fest Opens as Chair Sue Wang Says ‘Culture Is Power’ Amid AI Shift
Main Body Text:
Sue Wang , chair of the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), opened the seventh Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ) in Taipei on Friday by saying artificial intelligence is reshaping how the creative industries, and even human society, are defined.

“We are all asking: Does cultural content still have a future?” Wang said.

She said AI could take on technical tasks but could not replace the elements of creative work that move people. Wang urged Taiwan to put its technology strengths to work in ways that serve people and improve their lives. “I hope more people believe that culture is power. Especially in this rapidly changing era, cultural content can help create a happier society,” she said. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Wang also called this year’s edition an important milestone for the industry. “Everyone is working hard to build partnerships and integration, both horizontally and vertically. Cross-sector, cross-platform and cross-border collaboration has become a trend,” she said.

The event features 107 Market exhibitors from seven countries and 92 project and story pitches spanning film, series, animation, documentaries, publishing and comics. Industry participants from 28 countries are attending. The four-day Forum will hold 12 sessions with more than 20 speakers, addressing international co-production, streaming-platform consolidation, IP, short-form content and AI.

Hosted by Taiwanese actor Allison Lin, the opening ceremony was attended by Culture Minister Li Yuan; Wang Ting-an, executive secretary of the National Development Fund under the Executive Yuan; Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah; Toei Company President and CEO Yoshimura Fumio; Frédéric Laplanche, director of the French Office in Taipei; Fernando Mariano Schmidt Hernández, director of the Chilean Trade Office in Taipei; and Marco Lombardi of the Italian Economic, Trade and Cultural Promotion Office in Taipei, among many other local and international luminaries.

Li, who chaired the evaluation committee at TCCF’s first edition, said he had watched the event grow from an exhibition into a market and an international platform. “Now we’re thinking about the future of Taiwan’s cultural content ecosystem and how TCCF can become an Asian creative-content brand, helping cultural workers across Asia and around the world find opportunities and funding. That is one of the key goals behind the Ministry of Culture and TAICCA,” he said.

TCCF runs Nov. 6-9 at Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, Hall 2.

Title: Taiwan Should Bet on Horror to Crack Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s Biggest Film Market, Study Finds
Main Body Text:
Horror stands out as a natural meeting ground for Taiwanese and Indonesian producers, according to a K7 Media study of the Indonesian film and TV market presented by Trang Nguyen at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

The stakes are considerable. Indonesia is Southeast Asia’s largest economy and its biggest film market, with box office revenue of $352.9 million in 2025, according to figures drawn from PwC, Box Office Mojo and CJ CGV Vietnam. That is 1.6 times the size of Vietnam’s box office and five times Thailand’s. The market’s 5.1% compound annual growth rate also beats the Asia-Pacific average of 4.3%. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Local films rule the multiplexes. Indonesian titles made up 201, or 43%, of 2025 releases but took 64% of admissions, with 82.6 million tickets sold, per Cinepoint data via the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM). That is more than double the 36.9 million admissions for the 100 U.S. releases. Other Asian imports barely registered: 27 Japanese films drew 3.3 million admissions, while 61 Korean and 16 Chinese titles each pulled in 2 million.

Three local titles sit in the 10 million-plus club: Imajinari’s 2025 comedy “Agak Laen: Menyala Pantiku!,” Visinema’s 2025 animated fantasy adventure “Jumbo” and MD Pictures’ 2022 horror “KKN di Desa Penari.”

Horror is the genre Indonesia produces most for cinemas. Five of the 10 most-attended Indonesian films since 2011 are horror pictures, and recent hits have mixed scares with comedy or drama. Many of the country’s horror films draw on existing IP. Foreign horror can break out too. Korean hit “Exhuma” drove up local theatrical interest in Korean films after its 2024 run. The presentation singled out “The Rope Curse 4” as a recent Taiwan-Indonesia collaboration.

Remakes form a second route. The Indonesian version of Korean film “Miracle in Cell No. 7” sold around 5.8 million tickets in 2022 and went on to generate a new sequel plus an animated offshoot. “Kang Mak from Pee Mak,” a local take on Thai horror-comedy “Pee Mak,” drew around 4.9 million in 2024. Adaptations need not be film-to-film: a local big-screen version of “Descendants of the Sun,” the 2016 Korean series, is in production for cinemas in 2027.

On television, five commercial groups lead. MNC Group runs RCTI, MNCTV and GTV alongside streamers RCTI+ and Vision+ and microdrama app V+Short. Emtek/SCM operates SCTV, Indosiar and Mentari TV plus streamer Vidio. Trans Media (Trans TV, Trans7), Viva (ANTV, tvOne) and MD Entertainment (MDTV) round out the field.

Sinetron, the local soap format, remains the backbone of Indonesian TV series. The serials are churned out in bulk, usually screen every day or several nights a week, and often stretch to hundreds of episodes. Recent examples include RCTI’s “Terikat Janji,” which bowed in April 2026, and Indosiar’s “Merangkai Kisah Indah,” which launched in July 2025. Religious and faith-themed drama also features, with examples including RCTI’s “Amanah Wali” and SCTV’s “Istiqomah Cinta.” Streamers, by contrast, are packaging romance in shorter runs for younger viewers, leaning on existing digital IP and making crime, revenge and action a signature of premium programming.

Vidio, which launched in 2014, is Indonesia’s largest streaming platform by cumulative reach as of 2026. It released its first local original in 2019, grew fast during the pandemic and has teamed with Wattpad to turn web novels into series. Netflix arrived in 2016 but was blocked by state-owned telecom Telkom until 2020. It has since become the leading international streamer in the country, with “The Cigarette Girl” in 2023 as its first Indonesian original. Disney+ launched in 2020 as Disney+ Hotstar, rebranded in October 2025 and signed a deal with Vidio in October 2026 for a joint package. Viu entered in 2016, while Chinese-owned platforms WeTV and iQiyi have moved aggressively into the market with Chinese-language drama libraries and growing local slates.

For sellers of finished tapes, streaming is the most open door. Korean shows made up 50% of Netflix Indonesia’s top 50 most-watched titles between January and September 2026, ahead of Indonesian (22%), U.S. (14%) and Chinese (6%) fare. Thai series “To Love and Cherish” topped Viu Indonesia’s trending chart on Sept. 22, 2026, with Korean titles “Ok! Let’s Get Divorced” and “Reborn Rookie” behind it. Korean series “My Dearest Nemesis” became Vidio’s best-performing Korean drama after the platform bought exclusive first-run rights in 2025.

Among linear broadcasters, MDTV and ANTV both have an appetite for imports. MDTV runs a daily Korean drama double bill and “Marisol,” while ANTV programs Indian series including “Jaane Anjaane” and “Naagin 7.”

Microdrama is crossing over into the mainstream. RCTI brought microdramas to broadcast television in January 2026, slotting them in daily at 3:30 p.m. MNC Digital Entertainment launched V+Short in June 2026, pairing international titles with homegrown productions from across Southeast Asia. In September 2026, Vidio partnered with ReelShort to add more than 200 of its titles dubbed into Bahasa Indonesia.

In unscripted, local programs include popular Indosiar singing show “Dangdut Academy,” MNCTV game show “Uang Kaget Lagi” and Trans7 comedy variety show “Lapor Pak!” Imported formats remain few and mostly come from established Western franchises. Game shows and quizzes accounted for half of the unscripted formats brought into Indonesia between 2023 and 2026, followed by talent (25%), dating (13%), cooking (6%) and comedy (6%). Scripted remakes are still rare, though Vidio’s original series version of CJ ENM’s “Bad Guys” points to fresh interest.

In children’s content, animation that teaches, stays family-friendly and centers on likable characters does best, and linear channels stick with proven IP. Streaming has overtaken TV for kids’ viewing, with YouTube Kids a popular destination, and government regulation puts a premium on trusted, age-appropriate programming.

Taiwan’s own foothold is narrow. “Meteor Garden” remains a cultural touchstone from the 2000s, but beyond it there is little nostalgic goodwill for Taiwanese content to draw on, and many viewers can’t tell a Taiwanese series from a mainland Chinese or Hong Kong one. Taiwanese streamer Catchplay+ operates in Indonesia, but its reputation rests on Hollywood movies, not Taiwanese or wider Asian drama.

Beyond horror, the K7 Media study flagged foreign-drama specialist channels and streamers as targets for finished dramas, alongside IP adaptations into films and scripted series, Bahasa-language educational kids’ content delivered digitally and the film sector more broadly. It also urged Taiwanese companies to look past straight content sales and raise their profile through more promotional activity. The presentation pointed to JAFF Market, which will run Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta, as a place to start building ties with the local film industry.

Title: Tyler Perry Joins Keisha Lance Bottoms’ Georgia Transition Team Despite Director’s Sexual Assault Lawsuits
Main Body Text:
On Tuesday night, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the 2026 Georgia gubernatorial election, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor of any U.S. state and Georgia’s first Black governor.

One of the first moves made by Bottoms, who’d previously served as the mayor of Atlanta, a member of Atlanta City Council and a senior advisor and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement under former President Biden, was announcing, “ Tyler Perry , an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta,” as part of her transition team. Title: Why Does Amazon Want a TV Show Starring Melania Trump?
Main Body Text:
Amazon , it seems, cannot get enough “Melania.” And at this moment, they feel like the only entity for whom that’s true.

The company has announced its plan to release a two-part documentary series about First Lady Melania Trump on Nov. 20; this follows on the stilettoed heels of their feature film documentary, “Melania,” released in theaters in January. Back then, director Brett Ratner’s film — while failing to recoup the astonishing $75 million Amazon spent on rights and marketing — did well for a documentary, earning some $16.6 million. But that film came amidst the seeming height of a cultural shift toward forever-Trumpism that began in November 2024 — one that has now been decisively ended. In the wake of the midterms offering a stunning nationwide repudiation of her husband, what’s left to say about Melania? Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

There’s reason beyond the shock Democratic Party victories from Kansas to South Carolina to suspect “Melania,” the series — which, Amazon promises, will be split into episodes following Melania’s experience of the 2024 presidential transition and then the immediate aftermath of Donald Trump’s second inauguration — will meet an indifferent public. “Melania,” the film , covered the same territory with astounding vacuity. This viewer went in not expecting my opinions of Melania’s husband to shift but curious about the by-every-indication extraordinary life Melania herself has led. And I grew numb at the umpteenth shot of her walking into and out of rooms, random stylists and decorators burbling away in her wake.

Even by this family’s low standard, it seemed shameless: Melania Trump was willing to accept a staggeringly large check but seemed not to feel even the slightest twinge that would have prompted her to offer something, anything, to earn the fee. But the film was a document of an aesthetic, and a movement, that was ascendant.

The day after the 2024 election, a perception began spreading that the surprising nature of Trump’s popular-vote victory meant that not merely was Trump more popular than ever before but that our society had fundamentally changed. In Trump’s first term and through the Joe Biden presidency, corporations took tones between studied neutrality and resistance. Now, though, corporate America flocked to Trump, with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his soon-to-be-wife Lauren Sánchez among the guests of honor at Trump’s inauguration. As such, a film about how Melania prepared for said inauguration had a grim civic-duty feel. Want to see America? This was it — an oligarch’s wife flatly bragging to camera that she’s always had an intuitive feel for design, and charging you for the privilege of being in her company.

Something’s shifted! Trump is still the president (and Melania still the first lady), but we’ve just been issued as striking notice as possible that whatever change Trump has lost control of the national conversation. (Notable, perhaps: “Melania” came out in theaters before the launch of the disastrous war in Iran, a turning point for the president’s popularity.) This ought to have been predictable: Beyond the fact that Trump’s own tendencies seemed likely to doom his popularity sooner or later, no moment in time lasts forever, and electoral victories are just that, not restructures of society at every level.

This may be a hard pill to swallow for Bezos in particular, whose gut-renovation of his public image seemed designed to earn himself and his wife permanent seats at Mar-a-Lago. (Bezos’ tasteless June 2025 wedding, commandeering seemingly the entire city of Venice, was a stunning let-them-eat-cake moment from the onetime nerdy Seattle bookseller.) Amazon has, reportedly, discussed rebooting Trump’s old reality franchise “The Apprentice” with Donald Trump Jr. as its lead. Now that making the president happy seems like a less urgent concern — and that the negative optics of currying favor with him seem clear — one wonders how committed Bezos is to the new values he discovered in 2024.

An “Apprentice” reboot wouldn’t just be politically toxic at this moment, it’d never work: Everyone knows the only Trump who’s any good on TV is Donald. Just look at “Melania” — its subject seems to be gritting her teeth in order to get through a film designed to show her in an exclusively flattering light. But Amazon already spent the money they spent on it, and recutting it into a TV series will give Trump something to talk about. Increasingly distracted, the President spent the run-up to the election discussing men’s physiques and the day after his electoral thumping touring his under-construction ballroom ; being able to spin a story about his wife now having the highest-rated TV series on streaming, or whatever, will at least give him something to do, while the rest of the country tunes out.

But the project is symbolic of a series of bets corporate America made that Trump’s opposition would never win again. Oops! At Skydance, for instance, opinion journalist Bari Weiss, in charge of CBS News, has radically revamped the division into something that suited the moment for, well, a moment, and now couldn’t seem less like what viewers crave. And, more consequentially, the new Democratic Senate majority is signaling that they will, after taking over in January 2027, subpoena tech companies — including Amazon — over their donations to Trump’s ballroom project. The donations made, somewhat like the $75 million spent on a documentary that’s now a time capsule, are the kind companies make when thinking only in the present tense. And, this past week, they collided with a future in which buying off the powerful may not work as well. At least Amazon will always have footage of Melania Trump singing “Billie Jean” to Brett Ratner, for whatever that’s worth.

Title: ‘African Kung-Fu Nazis’ Franchise Lands at Hong Kong’s Cappu Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
International sales on cult martial arts splatter comedy “ African Kung-Fu Nazis ,” its sequel and a behind-the-scenes documentary have gone to Hong Kong-based Cappu Films .

The deal, struck with filmmaker and producer Sebastian Stein of Humanmade Films, was unveiled on the sidelines of Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. It covers “African Kung-Fu Nazis I,” “African Kung-Fu Nazis II” and the feature documentary “African Kung-Fu Nazis – The Doc.” It applies only to rights and territories that are still open, and leaves deals already in place untouched. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Japanese distributor Transformer gave both features a theatrical run in Japan, opening the original in June 2021 and the sequel four years later in July 2025. Busch Media Group handled the first film’s German release on DVD, Blu-ray and VOD. The sequel played Sitges’ Brigadoon sidebar in 2025. In 2026 it went on to the Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival (BIFFF), Grossmann and Macabro, where it picked up an honorable mention.

Mixing kung fu action, gore, horror and dark comedy, the series takes its cues from vintage Hong Kong martial arts films and from Ghana’s independent filmmaking scene. In the first film, Ghanaian kung fu fighters square off against send-ups of wartime figures from Germany and Japan, among them Adolf Hitler, Hideki Tojo and “Horseman” Goering.

The sequel teams one-armed fighter Addo with Sek Tin to take on cyborg “Adolf Robotler,” who wants to become president of Ghana. Stein said the film, a Ghana-Japan-Germany production shot mostly in Ghana, was paid for largely through crowdfunding, with Japanese fans of the first film providing much of the backing.

“African Kung-Fu Nazis – The Doc” goes behind the camera on the original, following the independent shoot that started the franchise.

“With their love for Chinese kung fu, our Ghanaian heroes smash the threat of fascism,” said Stein, CEO of Humanmade Films. “Total freedom, beautiful madness. Because you won’t drink champagne if you don’t take a risk!”

Cappu and the filmmakers also plan a line of art-led merchandise, to be produced via sister company Winners Gallery and built on the franchise’s characters and look, as part of the international marketing push. Concepts and release plans have yet to be finalized.

“We love fiercely independent horror and cult films, and we want to support filmmakers who are doing something that is entirely their own,” said Janice Woo of Cappu Films. “There’s a real love of kung fu cinema in these films. We come from production ourselves, so we understand how much it takes to get a film like this made. We’re excited to work with Sebastian and help bring all three films to more audiences.”

Cappu also operates out of Beijing and handles select releases in its home market and mainland China. Its slate ranges from Tony Leung Chiu-wai crime thriller “Fox Hunt” to Shan Jiang’s “Ephemera,” a 2026 Tribeca Festival U.S. Narrative Competition premiere. The lineup also includes Carter Ward’s romance “Step Back, Doors Closing” and Francesco Lucente’s fantasy adventure “Sinbad,” which DNEG is co-financing and producing.

Title: ‘Drummer Boy’ Review: Love, Family and Revolution Conflict at Musket’s Point in a Swoony Period Musical
Main Body Text:
This latest collaboration between Angel Studios and Christian pop group For King + Country is a pleasant if simplistic take on the United States’ foundational struggle for independence.

Arriving a bit late to ride the fizzled momentum of the nation’s semiquincentennial, and a bit early for Christmas, patriotic musical “ Drummer Boy ” nonetheless should strike a chord with Christian audiences. It’s the first feature for several collaborators since 2024’s “Unsung Hero,” one of the bigger “faith-based entertainment” hits in recent years, though this tale set at the outset of the Revolutionary War is a considerably different enterprise. “Hamilton,” it’s not. Still, for those seeking a more sentimentally earnest take on early U.S. history with a more vanilla contemporary-pop sound, the latest release from Angel Studios provides a confident, mostly pleasing throwback to original screen musicals of yore. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“Drummer Boy” will largely appeal to preexisting fans of Grammy-winning Christian music act For King + Country — comprising brothers Luke and Joel David Smallbone , the latter of whom both stars and co-directs with third Smallbone brother Ben. Viewers preferring wholly secular entertainment may find it on the hokey side, but should appreciate that religious messaging is relatively soft-pedaled here in favor of a more generalized plea for societal “forgiveness and reconciliation” — something arguably well-timed in the immediate wake of a contentious midterm election.

A 1762 prologue finds two families sailing from England to its colonies across the Atlantic. Their children are about the same age, but otherwise the groups are quite different: The Clems (led by Ioan Guffudd’s father Nathaniel) are humble folk hoping to “truly be free” in a new land hopefully void of class and other divisions. Whereas widowed Lord Balfour (Charles Esten) fully expects to carry his homeland’s aristocratic traditions abroad, complete with an apparent Black slave for his hoity-toity young daughter. Once in sight of land at last, the ship is attacked (by the French, as this is during the French and Indian War), with consequences falling hardest on the Clems.

Twelve years later, both clans have settled in Kingston, New York, that state’s eventual first capital. The Clems have established a grain mill, worked by mother Rachel (Melora Hardin) with now-grown sons Jeremiah (Joel David Smallbone) and Benjamin (Lucas Leach) — the latter still lamed by their fateful ocean crossing. Far above them in social station are the Balfours, who exert considerable political influence from a stately manse.

There, princessy only-child Elisabeth aka Lizzie (Beth Easdown) weighs her options as the region’s most sought-after debutante, while attended by servants including Emmaline (India Brown) and older Margaret (Beverley Knight). The latter pair hope one day to buy their liberty, Emmaline also pinning romantic hopes on Jeremiah, who once secretly taught her to read and write. For the time being, however, he only has eyes for pretty, fickle Lizzie. (An early scene in which she’s belle of a small ball provides the film’s sole major dance opportunity.)

Soon they’ve all got more pressing concerns, as excess taxation and other colonialist abuses from distant England’s rule trigger the War for Independence. Citizens are bitterly divided, rebel-friendly Ben’s big mouth getting the Clems branded as “traitors” by those loyal to the Crown. Lest that kill off the family business, Jeremiah makes amends by signing up as a British Army redcoat under Lord Balfour’s command. They’re soon sent off to fight, and in angry pique Ben too leaves home, fast landing in the company of Patriot colonist forces led by Scotsman Major Ambrose (Iain Glen). He’s rejected at first due to disability, then proves his value with an impromptu drum solo — back then, percussionists issued the “charge command” and other signals to troops when ordered.

Thus is set up a core, somewhat corny “brother versus brother” conflict, duly culminating in instances where the Clem brethren must face each other on the battlefield. Meanwhile back in town, Emmaline plays Cyrano — writing letters to Jeremiah that he assumes are from Lizzie, who in fact has already more or less forgotten him. This covert communication will lead to trouble, exacerbating racial inequities even as Lord Balfour eventually, foolishly brings the war back to his own doorstep.

“Drummer Boy” avoids staging full-scale battles, though its hectic skirmishes in forests and such are probably an accurate-enough reflection of how the war was really won. (The more formal, rule-bound British fighting style was famously ignored and undermined by Yanks’ guerrilla tactics.) But then this is not exactly a grittily realistic flashback, or one terribly concerned with details of historical timeline.

Indeed, the 18th century looks very scrubbed and pretty here, Cathal Watters’ handsome widescreen cinematography at times recalling the more idealizing 19th-century landscape painters. Never mind that these particular landscapes are sometimes rather obviously Ireland rather than upstate New York. (Angel Studios’ recent “Young Washington” was also shot in Ireland, where the past is better preserved.) Nadine Powell’s costumes and Chad Krowchuk’s production design likewise offer serviceable period fidelity while suggesting our nation’s birth came very freshly laundered.

The dramatics, too, are awfully neat, but they work well enough in an idiom of teen-friendly romance and apolitical strife. (It is all but suggested at the close here that the Revolutionary War ended because both sides realized war wasn’t nice.) This is a musical in a very mainstream pop mode of supple but almost juvenile high voices singing banal lyrics to catchy melodies with rather bombastic production. There are some attractive small-string-ensemble elements to the arrangements of both the songs by For King + Country and the backing score by Garrett P. Tyler ad Danny Lopez.

But otherwise “Drummer Boy” makes no attempt to sound “period,” and the anachronism squeaks by because the emotions milked are also very Millennial-and-beyond, with those songs mostly limning “Dear Diary”-type internal monologue sentiments of personal aspiration and pining. Even the major theme of interracial love is handled with such romanticized discretion, neither race nor slavery ever actually get mentioned. As far as religious content goes, it’s a given that everyone here is Christian, but Richard L. Ramsey’s efficient screenplay treats the central conflicts as matters of human morality (or lack thereof), rather than tests of faith.

The young leads make appealing impressions within the uncomplicated limits of the script and the ten songs (which include a few adaptions of traditional hymns), though one might wish the soldier-sidekicks the two brothers get were given more to do — a subplot or two wouldn’t have hurt. The older performers are largely wasted in one-dimensional roles, Glen faring best among them.

It is a tribute to the co-directors’ sincerity and polish that a heavily contrived, snowy Christmas climax on the field of battle stretches credulity to the breaking point, but somehow that doesn’t matter much. Not a movie for the cynical, “Drummer Boy” won’t convert anyone not already inclined towards the outputs of Angel Studios or For King + Country. But the previously converted should be highly gratified, and everyone else is likely to find this throwback pleasant, if a tad innocuous.

Title: ‘Entertainment Tonight’ Sees Big Ratings Gains This Fall, Following ‘Access Hollywood’ Cancellation (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
“ Entertainment Tonight ” is widening its lead as the No. 1 syndicated newsmagazine, averaging 2.99 million viewers during the week of Oct. 5, according to Nielsen live+same-day ratings.

That week was significant to the CBS Media Ventures-produced and distributed “Entertainment Tonight,” as it coincided with the CBS network’s primetime premiere week, which was up 9% vs. CBS premiere week in 2025. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Meanwhile, “Entertainment Tonight” is also enjoying double-digit year-to-year growth for the first month of the TV season (from Sept. 28 to Oct. 25) in major demos. CBS Media Ventures hasn’t done the analysis, but the bump does coincide with the end of rival syndicated entertainment newsmag “ Access Hollywood ,” which ended its run on Sept. 11 after 30 seasons (and after NBCUniversal eliminated its first-run syndication division).

Whatever the reason, for the first month of the season in Nielsen live+same day, “Entertainment Tonight” Season 46 averaged 2.88 million viewers, up 8% from last year (2.67 million), as well as a 0.27 rating with adults 18-49, up 37% from last year (0.20). In adults 25-54, the show was up 23% (from 0.32 to 0.39 rating).

And in key women demos, the jumps were also huge: In women 25-54, the rating was 0.47 (up 32% from 0.36), and in women 18-49, the rating was 0.30, up 38% from 0.22.

“Forty-six seasons in, this team still asks one question every day: Why watch us tonight? The answer is access no one else can get and a half-hour that moves,” said “Entertainment Tonight” exec producer Erin Johnson. “Watching a new generation of viewers find us is exciting.”

The ratings bumps come as “Entertainment Tonight” just won its eighth consecutive Daytime Emmy for outstanding entertainment news series. The show has won 11 overall in the category.

“ET” is co-hosted by Kevin Frazier and Nischelle Turner. Correspondents are Cassie DiLaura, Denny Directo and Emily Curl. Working with exec producer Johnson are Whitney Wallace and Leslie Kawaguchi, who serve as co-executive producers.

Title: ‘Good Boy’ Filmmaker Ben Leonberg to Direct Movie Adaptation of Horror Novella ‘Look Out’ for Republic Pictures (EXCLUSIVE)
