Title: ‘Jimmy’ Review: Cornball James Stewart Biopic Gets the Manner, but Not the Man
Main Body Text:
KJ Apa does a passable Stewart impression in this one-note, semi-faith-based portrait, which mainly portrays the beloved Hollywood star as a vessel for patriotic values.

As one of Hollywood’s staunchest Republicans, the late James Stewart perhaps wouldn’t be rolling in his grave in response to “ Jimmy ,” a biopic that — in focusing rather less on his artistry than on his military service — paints him in a glowingly conservative light. But either way, he deserves better than this hokey, superficial portrait, which lives up to the popular conception of Stewart as an all-American mensch and everyman hero, while finding precious little of interest to actually say about him, either as a human or as an icon. It’s buoyed by “Riverdale” star KJ Apa ‘s enthusiastic but thin portrayal, which mostly captures the star’s signature drawl and aw-shucks persona — but, like the film itself, grants him only a sentimental semblance of a soul. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Directed by Aaron Burns — whose previous two features were both produced by the streaming arm of Christian studio Affirm Films — and released by Fathom Entertainment, “Jimmy” isn’t explicitly faith-based, but it is at least faith-adjacent, with much emphasis on Stewart’s Presbyterian background, and more than one moment of religious epiphany when the chips are down. Not by accident is its most detailed glimpse of its subject’s Hollywood career a reconstruction of the famous bridge prayer scene in “It’s a Wonderful Life” — the scene that Stewart himself identified as his favorite from all his films.

These are all unsurprising choices to make in depicting a star who was largely loved by the public for his air of very ordinary decency, and whose career was marked by a rejection of Hollywood glamour and decadence in favor of family values and patriotic duty. But “Jimmy” conveys none of these qualities from the inside out, instead making its eponymous protagonist a bland vessel for a kind of one-size-fits-all virtue. As written by Justin Strawhand and played by Apa, Stewart isn’t so much the everyman of American cinema as an interchangeable nice guy with admittedly distinctive vocal mannerisms; when the film does try to get under his skin, it lands on a fairly generic snapshot of WWII-related PTSD.

It opens in medias res , with Stewart being pitched the idea for “It’s a Wonderful Life” by close friend and fellow Second World War serviceman Frank Capra (Max Casella) — and not being altogether sold on Capra’s claim that “a hundred years from now, this film will be remembered.” (That the director is almost certainly correct doesn’t excuse such strenuously on-the-nose writing.) We rewind five years: It’s 1941, and Stewart, fresh from his Academy Award win for “The Philadelphia Story,” has just received his draft letter from the U.S. Army. Louis B. Mayer (a ripe Jason Alexander) waves it away, keen that the star capitalize on his post-Oscar glory, while venomous gossip columnist Hedda Hopper (Sarah Drew) reports that Stewart has dodged the draft.

Stewart is further goaded by his stern, salt-of-the-earth father (Neal McDonough), who dismisses his son’s military aspirations in amusingly sneery fashion: “Go back to Hollywood and make peace with the fact that you are what you are.” Determined to serve, he finally enlists in the Air Force, cuing a five-year screen hiatus when America is pulled into the war, and he’s stationed in England as a bomber pilot for the 453rd Bombardment Group. There, he bonds with the less famous men under his command, engages in aerial combat that is shot in synthetic video game style, and enters into a tedious, fictionalized romance with brittly aristocratic Englishwoman Julia (Kara Killmer). And so the erstwhile movie star effectively lives a movie for a change, instead of making one.

None of this is particularly enlightening, and any opportunity to portray the conflict between Stewart’s celebrity, soldierly and civilian identities is squandered by the consistently phony, ennobling tone of proceedings. Our hero speaks mostly in clunky platitudes (“I’d like to look at myself in the mirror and see a good man looking back at me,” “I don’t want to be a god, I want to be man”) that wind up making him a bit of a pill. Besides, we hardly feel the seismic shift in worlds from backlot to battle, since DP James Mather applies the same smoothly gilded finish throughout; you can sense the camera rolling in every frame of the film, whether it’s capturing Hollywood artifice or not. At his lowest, most trauma-ridden point on the “It’s a Wonderful Life” shoot, Stewart is given advice that snaps him back into form: “What the audience needs is truth — are you brave enough to give it to them?” Jimmy ultimately is; “Jimmy,” not so much.

Title: ‘Kamen Rider’ Studio Toei Frames Generative AI Rules, Sets First Video Games for 2027
Main Body Text:
Toei , the Japanese studio giant behind “ Kamen Rider ” and the Super Sentai series that became “Power Rangers,” has drawn up rules for generative AI and started using AI in its film and video production, president and CEO Yoshimura Fumio said at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

A dedicated team at the company is testing how far AI can be used in actual content production, and Toei is building an AI system that helps less experienced producers estimate budgets. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“We have put in place rules for the use of generative AI, and from this year we have started using AI in our film and video production,” Yoshimura said. “We are already working on things like creating backgrounds with AI.”

Toei’s back-office departments also use AI for routine tasks, data processing and internal queries, and the company is looking at applying it to the creative supervision of IP merchandise. Yoshimura pointed to “Dreams of Violets,” a live-action feature made entirely with generative AI that was selected for the Tribeca Festival in June. The 75-minute film was reportedly made by two creators for around $2,000.

“I believe AI is not something that takes away jobs, but a tool that expands the possibilities of expression and business,” he said.

Toei also put a timeline on its move into games. Toei Games, the label launched this year to mark the company’s 75th anniversary, will release “Hino” in early 2027, with “Killa” and “Debug Nephemee” following from spring 2027. All three are original titles from outside creators rather than adaptations of Toei IP, and will launch on Steam before rolling out to Nintendo Switch, PlayStation and Xbox.

“We aim to bring game creators’ talent on board over the long term as a new vein of IP creation, and make games the starting point for stories in place of novels and comics,” Yoshimura said.

The keynote also mapped out how Toei is taking “Kamen Rider,” which turned 55 this year, beyond Japanese TV. Yoshimura held up the franchise as his main example of what the company calls the “evergreening” of IP. The first series premiered in 1971, and the Showa-era shows that ran until 1988 built its core fanbase. The Heisei-era series that began in 2000 handed the franchise down from parents to children, while events, merchandise, manga, anime and stage shows have since carried it to a third generation.

The current series, “Kamen Rider Zeztz,” was rolled out almost simultaneously around the world, including Taiwan, the rest of Asia and North America, which Yoshimura called a big step for the group. Toei is also pushing into India. “Kamen Rider” was introduced there at a Japanese IP event in 2025, and the strong response led to a deal with a local Disney-affiliated company.

“Considering the population size and rising incomes from a growing middle class, I think India can be called an extremely promising market in the medium to long term,” Yoshimura said. “We expect it will take time before this takes root as a business, but it’s important to build connections now and steadily grow our partnerships and fan base.”

In April, Toei launched The Kamen Rider Animated, an animation label. Its first project teams the studio with Aniplex, the company behind “Demon Slayer,” and Shirogumi, which worked on Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus One,” on a new “Kamen Rider” property with a scale and style of action only animation can deliver. A live-action label, The Kamen Rider Premium, will make full-scale hero action films for a wider audience, including international viewers and people who don’t follow the TV shows.

Under its Toei New Wave 2033 medium- to long-term plan, the company aims to raise the share of its sales that comes from overseas from 30% to 50%, with Asia the current focus. Yoshimura cited estimates that the global entertainment and media market is growing by an average of 3.4% a year. He added that streaming now lets K-pop, Japanese anime, Indian films and Chinese microdramas travel the world without being changed.

“Now that content rooted in local cultures and histories, like ‘Shogun,’ is crossing racial and national borders and captivating people around the world, I’d say the main battlefield for our business is overseas,” he said.

During the audience Q&A, Yoshimura said that before “Power Rangers,” Toei exported its Japanese series unchanged, and they struggled to win over Western audiences. The breakthrough came from keeping only the characters and rebuilding the cast and drama in the U.S.

“I believe this approach of localization is indispensable for spreading characters around the world,” he said. “We also understand that, unlike animation, live-action work in particular is not something that is readily accepted as-is in each country.”

“Power Rangers” has now run in the U.S. for more than 30 years. In 2025, the original “Mighty Morphin Power Rangers” was relaunched as “Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Re-Ignition,” with newly designed toys from Hasbro, a “Fortnite” collaboration and a Lego line in the works. Toei used a similar remake model in the Philippines. “Voltes V: Legacy,” the 2023 live-action version of Toei’s 1977 anime “Super Electromagnetic Machine Voltes V,” peaked at a 58% rating there and was released in Japanese cinemas the following year.

The company is also building stories from scratch in other markets. In February, it signed a strategic co-production partnership with Thai producer-distributor M Studio. Together with M Studio and Korea’s Showbox, it is adapting Ito Junji’s “Long Hair in the Attic” as a premium Thai film for Asian audiences. The film will open in Thailand first before heading to Japan and other territories.

In co-production, Toei backed “Dear Stranger,” a Japan-Taiwan-U.S. film from director Mariko Tetsuya that stars Gwei Lun-mei and Nishijima Hidetoshi. It was shot entirely in New York and released last September. The project was selected for the Hong Kong Asia Film Financing Forum’s HAF and raised money abroad from the start, with Taiwanese investors including TAICCA’s TICP 2.0 program. Toei’s Kyoto studio is also supporting the Japan shoot of “Iris,” an action thriller from a U.S. independent producer.

Toei is the only company in Japan that owns and runs two studio lots, one in Tokyo and one in Kyoto. The Tokyo lot houses Japan’s only permanent 270-degree LED volume stage.

Toei is also making short-form content. “Everyday Host Club” is a short anime of 24 episodes that run about three minutes each. “Meshimori Onna,” produced at the Kyoto studio for a client, is a vertical period drama of 30 episodes that run one to two minutes. Yoshimura suggested that vertical formats could one day become the norm even in cinemas.

On Taiwan, he noted that in 2025 Japanese films were the most-released titles in the market and second only to U.S. films at the box office. Toei titles released there include “Midnight Diner,” “Shin Kamen Rider,” “Howling Village” and “Oshi no Ko.” Local broadcaster YoYo TV airs “Kamen Rider,” and Toei is expanding live character shows in Taiwan with a local partner. The studio also invested in the Taiwanese horror film “The Rope Curse 4.” Yoshimura said he wants long-term tokusatsu partnerships and international co-productions with Taiwan.

“We are looking for partners with whom we can plan, make and deliver compelling stories to the world together,” he said.

Yoshimura joined Toei in 1988. He worked in live events, licensing and digital distribution, including some of Japan’s early mobile content and subscription streaming services, and became president in 2023.

Title: ‘Lord of the Rings,’ ‘Avatar’ VFX House Weta FX Partners With Taiwan’s Moonshine Studio Under AI Pact With TAICCA
Main Body Text:
Weta FX , the New Zealand visual effects company behind “The Lord of the Rings ” and “Avatar,” is partnering with Taiwanese animation and VFX outfit Moonshine Studio.

The investment is part of a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency ( TAICCA ) aimed at making Taiwan an AI hub for Asia’s content industries.

Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah and TAICCA chair Sue Wang signed a memorandum of understanding on Friday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Taiwan’s Minister of Culture Li Yuan attended the signing. No figure was given for the investment. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Seah said the partnership has three parts. The first is the partnership with Moonshine, founded by Lin Chia-chi, which he said had been around six months in the making. The second is a technology platform that will invest in Taiwanese film and TV projects and use Weta FX’s global reach to get them in front of wider audiences.

“On the AI road, nobody is really far, far ahead,” Seah said. “We all have to venture into this tech-filled AI world together. That’s why, while investing in Taiwan, we’re investing in technology.”

The third part, and the one Seah said he values most, is talent. A program will allow Taiwanese filmmakers, particularly young ones, to come to Weta FX for exchanges and internships, and potentially to work there in future.

Seah has spent close to 16 years as a VFX CEO. That includes 14 years running Digital Domain, the company co-founded by James Cameron. He moved to Peter Jackson’s Weta FX nearly two years ago. Li noted that Seah was born in Malaysia and grew up in New Taipei’s Yonghe district before working in China and Hong Kong.

Weta FX’s staff alone, Seah said, make up around 2% of the population of Wellington, New Zealand’s capital.

“Over the past 30 years, Weta turned Wellington from a political capital into such an important global production base,” Seah said. “We think Taiwan has even more of that opportunity.”

Wang said Moonshine’s team ranked first among Taiwan’s VFX houses. “Every time we met the Moonshine team, my only worry was: Can you make money like this? How long can you keep going?” she said. Wang added that the team “deserves to be put to better use, and seen by more people.”

Wang also thanked Taiwan’s National Development Fund for its support.

Li summed up the day in an eight-character Chinese phrase, “Daniel Seah comes home, dreams come true.” The phrase plays on Moonshine’s Chinese name, which means “dream.” He said AI and cultural technology will be among the Ministry of Culture’s priorities for the next four years.

Li joined Wang Film Productions at 37 hoping to make original animation, and gave up two to three years later. “I thought maybe this dream would take 20 or 30 years to come true,” he said. “I didn’t expect that after waiting so long, I would at least see it come true with my own eyes.”

Also on hand were TAICCA president Erica Wang and three Weta FX executives: chief technology officer Kimball Thurston, VFX supervisor Sheldon Stopsack and R&D head Andrew Moffat.

Title: ‘Musk’ Doc Gets International Release Dates
Main Body Text:
Universal has laid out its international rollout plans for Alex Gibey’s documentary about Elon Musk .

“ Musk ,” which comes in at a hefty 3 hours and 45 minutes, will begin its global release via Universal Pictures International in the U.K., where it hits cinemas on Jan. 15, followed by Germany on Jan. 21, Spain on Feb. 5, France on Feb. 17 and Australia on Feb. 25. Other territory release dates are to follow. The international rollout follows the documentary’s U.S. theatrical release through Bleecker Street in October. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

The news comes after Gibney said that the studio had wavered over its international release plans for the film , which has come under legal threats from the SpaceX founder. In an interview with the New York Times and questioned what had happened, the director said: “Were they concerned that in this political environment, a film about the world’s richest man was problematic? Maybe, but you have to ask them.”

“Musk,” which premiered in Venice and has received critical acclaim, seeks to make sense of the world’s richest man and the outsized influence he has on the world, diving deep into his shift to MAGA supporter, controversies surrounding his Occupy Mars mission and Tesla’s self-driving cars and his contentious relationships with several of the mothers of his 14 children.

Variety described it as a “lacerating and important watch, grounded in Alex Gibney ’s supremely insightful but user-friendly mastery of the documentary form.”

Its subject, meanwhile, called it a “hit piece” and said “dogshit is worth more respect.” He added that Gibney “has ZERO integrity” and is a “horrible human.”

Following stops in Toronto and London, “Musk” will continue its festival tour with upcoming stops at the Lisbon Film Festival, IDFA in Amsterdam and the Stockholm Film Festival later this month.

Title: ‘Pout-Pout Fish’ Studio Like a Photon Creative Unveils Seven-Film Animation Slate With Sola Media, Ahead of AFM (EXCLUSIVE)
Main Body Text:
Like a Photon Creative , the Australian animation studio behind “ The Pout-Pout Fish ,” has lined up seven new animated features and handed international distribution rights on the full slate to Sola Media.

Production finance comes from Elevate Production Finance and Alceon Entertainment Partners. Maslow Entertainment has picked up Australia and New Zealand distribution on the features. According to the companies, the lineup could create as many as 1,000 jobs in Australia and Ireland. Like a Photon Creative CEO Kristen Souvlis will attend the upcoming American Film Market ( AFM ). Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

First up is “Familiar,” an original developed in-house that will be made as a treaty co-production with Irish company Elephant Goldfish. Production on the film is expected to start in March 2027. Further titles will be revealed later.

The film is set at Ironclaw Academy, a school where the animal companions of sorcerers – known as familiars – go through a demanding and frequently messy training regime. Its central character is Josie, a feisty young cat.

“Families keep coming back to our films, and we’re focused on making projects that deserve that trust, with strong stories and broad appeal. ‘Familiar’ is the first of seven new features in our growing pipeline. Sola Media has a proven track record with our work, and together we see real opportunity to take Australian and European content to international audiences,” Souvlis said.

Alongside each of the seven features, the studio will make short-form direct-to-consumer material built from footage that won’t appear in the films themselves. That content will be bundled with the movies and rolled out across a range of online and social platforms.

The slate follows “The Pout-Pout Fish,” which Sola Media handled internationally. Adapted from the popular children’s book series, the film opened at No. 9 at the U.S. box office and currently ranks as the fourth highest-grossing Australian film of 2026. It also hit No. 1 on Amazon Prime Kids and No. 6 among all Prime viewers. Maslow released it in Australian cinemas on Jan. 1, with Viva Kids handling the U.S. release on March 20.

Sola Media will also oversee international distribution for the studio’s next release, “The Neverending Pillow Fort,” the first feature from Crayola Studios, produced with MIMO Studios. Allison Brownmoore directs the film, which is due in early 2027. Elizabeth Cullen and Sofia Rose voice best friends Maggie and Abby, with Guy Pearce, David Tennant, Teresa Palmer and Marsai Martin also in the cast.

Sola Media managing director Solveig Langeland said mixing humor and heart has always sat at the center of the studio’s storytelling, backed by its skill at bringing characters to life through strong voice casts. “We are proud of the successes we have achieved together and excited to embark on the next chapter of our partnership. With their expansion into co-productions with Ireland, Like a Photon is taking another exciting step forward. Their forward-thinking approach to building brands and engaging audiences through direct-to-consumer content from the earliest stages of production adds a powerful new dimension to their upcoming slate, creating awareness and marketing momentum long before the films reach cinemas,” she said.

Separately, Like a Photon Creative has teamed with Screen Queensland on the Escalate: Feature Focus Writers Initiative. Under the scheme, six screenwriters based in Queensland will each write a script for a possible 3D animated feature, working from concepts supplied by the studio. Writers’ rooms kick off in February 2027.

The studio has backed and made 10 animated features in 3D for worldwide theatrical release since 2017, among them “The Wishmas Tree,” “Combat Wombat” and its 2023 sequel, “Daisy Quokka: World’s Scariest Animal,” “The Sloth Lane” and “The Lost Tiger.” It also created the Sanctuary City multiverse for Universal Content Group.

Langeland founded Sola Media in 2004. The company, which has offices in Stuttgart and Munich, was acquired in 2020 by Embracer Group’s Plaion but continues to operate independently under Langeland and fellow managing director Moritz Peters.

Title: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Sets HBO Max Streaming Release Date
Main Body Text:
“ The End of Oak Street ” is coming to a neighborhood near you. The suburban dinosaur film is set for release on HBO Max on Nov. 13.

From director David Robert Mitchell, “The End of Oak Street” premiered in theaters on Aug. 14 from Warner Bros. Pictures. The film stars Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor as Denise and Greg Platt, the parents of a family that is magically transported into a prehistoric landscape. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

Armed with a baseball bat and a shotgun, the Platt family must survive the dinosaurs terrorizing their quaint 1980s neighborhood, rescue their family dog Starbuck and uncover what has happened to Oak Street. The dinosaur attacks have at least one upside, though, as running from the prehistoric beasts forces Denise and Greg to overcome their marital tension.

The film also stars Maisy Stella (“My Old Ass,” “Nashville”), Christian Convery (“Frankenstein,” “The Monkey”), Jordan Alexa Davis (“Defending Jacob,” ‘Thriller”), P.J. Byrne (“The Wolf of Wall Street,” “Babylon”) and Chris Coy (“Lanterns,” “Black Rabbit”).

The “Jurassic Park”-style romp with dinosaurs grossed $121 million during its theatrical run against its $80-92 million production budget. The film came toward the end of a blockbuster summer box office lineup , following hot on the heels of “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”

This is Mitchell’s first feature film since 2018’s “Under the Silver Lake.” A sequel to his supernatural horror “It Follows” was announced in 2023 and filming began this summer. Mitchell wrote, directed and produced “The End of Oak Street.” J.J. Abrams, Hannah Minghella, Jon Cohen, Matt Jackson and Tommy Harper also produced.

Title: ‘Trick ‘r Treat’ Director Michael Dougherty on the Joy of Designing Sam, His Signature Halloween Mascot, ‘Strictly for the Passion, Strictly for the Art’
Main Body Text:
Michael Dougherty really loves October 31.

“Some of my earliest memories were Halloween,” Dougherty said during a Variety -moderated production masterclass in partnership with genre festival FilmQuest in Provo, Utah. “Carving a pumpkin with my dad, going out trick-or-treating. That, combined with my love of horror movies and the occult, made me go down the Halloween rabbit hole and learn that it really is a strange, mystical holiday. It’s not just about putting on costumes and getting candy.” Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

During college, Dougherty landed on the idea for Sam, the costumed child who would become his mascot and a figurehead for Halloween. Sam would later end up being an integral part of the director’s 2007 anthology film “Trick ’r Treat.”

“In my mind, the spirit of Halloween would look like a child,” Dougherty said. “So that would allow it to roam door-to-door, knocking, seeing if you were obeying the rules and traditions of Halloween. It should be a costume that’s timeless, so there’s the scarecrow mask and the orange pajamas. But I love the idea that he’s mischievous and silent.”

Sam captivated Dougherty, who sought to bring him to life in a short film called “Season’s Greetings.”

“I made it as my senior thesis film when I was at NYU,” he said. “For most of 1995 into 1996, I drew this animated short by hand. Computers were just coming onto the scene, but I chose to suffer for my art and do it with pencil and paper and actually shoot it on 16mm film.”

This year marks the 30th anniversary of “Season’s Greetings,” and to celebrate, Dougherty did a 4K restoration of the short, which ended up becoming a sizable project on its own.

“I had some old 16mm film prints sitting in a closet, and I transferred them to digital right after I got out of NYU,” he said. “But the transfer even back then wasn’t that great. I thought, ‘Well, the 30th anniversary is coming up. Why not scan it at 4K?’ So I found this really great company in Hollywood called Origins Archival, and they painstakingly went in and scanned every single frame from the original 16 mm print. Then again, just choosing to suffer for my art, we went through every single frame and got rid of every piece of dust, dirt, scratch, stabilized it and they created this beautiful 4K DCP and it’s never looked or sounded better. I even took it back to my original composer and sound designer, Evan Chen, and he created a 5.1 track for it.”

Dougherty has faced difficulties in getting another “Trick ’r Treat” film made, as he said he has a great script but the modest budget is too frightening for a lot of people in the industry.

“It’s not low budget, but it would cost about what the first movie cost with inflation, which is roughly $20 million,” he said. “That number tends to scare a lot of accountants for whatever reason.”

That said, he’s been able to keep Sam’s spirit alive and well through other mediums, including a just-released graphic novel called “Trick ‘r Treat: Witching Hours,” as well as commissioning a series of Sam short films to be released on the character’s official Instagram page .

“I went around and found a bunch of other weirdos and misfits whose work I’ve admired over the years on Instagram and YouTube,” Dougherty said of the project. “I asked, ‘Hey, do you want to make some cool Sam stuff?’ It’s been a ton of fun.”

Despite having a winning Hollywood track record that includes films such as “Krampus” and “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” Dougherty’s recent work on “Season’s Greetings” reminded him of the early joy of creativity.

“I wasn’t just restoring the film, I was restoring a piece of my soul in the process,” he said. “It really did bring back memories. I wasn’t happy until they gave me every single frame of the scan, and I sat there for 10 hours a day sometimes. I was going in and removing the dust and scratches, or even reanimating portions of it and recovering portions of it. That drive really brought back memories of what it felt like to do it strictly for the passion, strictly for the art and not do it for a paycheck.”

Title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sparks Frenzy in Europe as  Screenings Sell Out and Anticipation Soars: ‘People Are Just Desperate to See It’
Main Body Text:
“ You Can See Everything ,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ’s smash-hit documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has yet to open in major international territories. But the crescendoing anticipation for a nearly three-hour film that came out of nowhere suggests that it could also rock numerous other box offices in the coming weeks.

In the U.K., where A24 is self-releasing the film, tickets began selling out a month before its opening on Nov. 20, prompting chains such as Picturehouse and Cineworld to add extra screenings. It’s a similar story in France, where distributor Metropolitan Filmexport has seen advance screenings sell out far ahead of its opening there on Dec. 30. Related Stories The Nielsen Tide: How SEC Teams Dominate College Football Viewership

“I’ve released hundreds of films and I’ve not known anything like it in terms of buzz — people are just desperate to see it,” says a distribution exec in the U.K. “I think it’s going to explode on Nov. 20. It’s going to be one of, if not the biggest documentary of all time, just based on pre-bookings.”

Excluding concert films, 2004’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” is still the most successful documentary in the U.K. (it’s currently the most successful globally), with a box office of £6.55 million ($8.8 million). It’s a figure many expect “You Can See Everything” to easily surpass.

A24 adopted a staggered release strategy in the U.S., more than tripling the amount of screens in its second weekend. But Variety hears that, to cope with the pent-up demand, it’ll likely bolt out of the British cinematic gates wide, going straight into around 500 cinemas.

In France, Victor Hadida, president of Metropolitan Filmexport, tells Variety that the company organized a nationwide series of sneak previews on Dec. 1 across roughly 100 theaters. Tickets sold out within hours.

“It’s crazy because we put tickets on sale on Saturday at 9 a.m., and some theaters were already sold out by noon,” says Hadida, whose slate also includes “The Debut.” “The demand is enormous and it hasn’t stopped. You can see it on social media, and you can see people going to theaters asking about the film.”

Unlike the U.K., Metropolitan Filmexport — which bought “You Can See Everything” from A24 at Toronto, shortly after it’s surprise Telluride premiere— will be following a similar progressive rollout to the U.S., opening in approximately 150 to 200 theaters before expanding based on demand.

Hadida says the nearly three-hour running time was a key factor in scheduling the release during the Christmas holidays, when moviegoers have more time to spare. Metropolitan is betting that the Dec. 1 previews will help build word of mouth — something that has been absolutely crucial in the film’s success so far — ahead of the official opening.

But by the time it comes out in France on Dec. 30, much of the rest of the world will already have had a chance to see it. After acquiring large swathes of Europe, Asia, the Middle East and South America for the film before the opening U.S. weekend, Sony has now revealed its release strategy for all of its 29 territories, with opening dates running from Nov. 19 through Dec. 9.

Thanks to cultural and language crossovers, not to mention a strong eye for documentary films, especially theatrically, there are high expectations for Scandinavia. Sony has the entire region, and opens across Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden in the space of 48 hours from Nov. 19. There are similar hopes for another major market, Germany (Dec. 3). Highlighting anticipation there, a recent CNN article told the story of a German fan who crossed the border to get to a preview screening in Poland (where it opens Nov. 6).

But with other territories such as India, Mexico, South Korea and Brazil on the rollout list and a film that continues to defy the norms or standard expectations, nothing should be ruled out.

As one exec notes: “You can’t sell any market short when something becomes cultural like this.”

In terms of actual promotional launch plans for “You Can See Everything,” talks are underway to fly Fielder and Oppenheim over to some of the more major premieres. However, as one publicity insider notes, since the film continues to enjoy a wildly unpredictable journey on home soil, plans are likely “very TBC.”

With the U.K. likely the biggest overseas market, London would seem a highly probable destination for the pair (Oppenheim was in town in October for the London Film Festival screening of “Primetime”). They’re both due to attend two BAFTA screenings in the capital next week, so assumingly will be stay in town for the premiere, although exact details of that are yet to be revealed. Hadida adds that Metropolitan is hoping to bring them to Paris in December as well.

But given the mystery around the film — not to mention some major spoilers to protect — there’s a limit to what anyone would want the filmmakers to actually talk about. Variety hears that the standard premiere media line would likely be scrapped, while any Q&As would likely be held just for awards voters (Fielder and Oppenheim will be taking part in Q&As at the BAFTA screenings in London)

“It’s so different to a lot of other PR plans and strategy, because you just don’t want to say anything,” says the publicity insider. “That’s why it’s all so minimal — you just want the film to speak for itself.”

Hadida in France also acknowledges that preserving the mystery — which has been a major element of A24’s marketing strategy — is key.

“Part of their approach is also not to reveal too much about the film, because what’s important about this experience is that you discover what the film is about at the same time as the filmmakers,” he says.

However, among the more eye-opening reveals in “You Can See Everything,” one that saw the film land an unexpected R-rating for “graphic nudity,” won’t be available to everyone. Due to censorship laws in Middle East, Variety hears that the scene in question — not critical but the source of much chatter — will have to be cut for it to be released.
